reads.title: Chartbook 465 The Last of the Magicians: Thomas Mann, John Maynard Keynes and the Alchemy of Bourgeois Liberalism
reads.subtitle: An essay by Adam Tooze and Stefan Eich
reads.body:
> The new, socialized world, the world of planning and co-operation, will come; humanity will get rid of unnecessary sufferings that are a disgrace to intelligence; and this will be achieved by a great and sober effort that has already enrolled under its banner all who have turned their backs upon a cult of musty, obscurantist, petty bourgeois sentiment. It will come; for a rational outward order of things in keeping with the present stage of human enlightenment must be created, or, if the worst happens, will be produced by violent convulsions. Only then can the heart reassert its rights with good conscience. The great sons of the bourgeois age, those whose capacity for spiritual growth raised them above the level of their class, are living proof of the fact that there are in the bourgeois nature infinite potentialities, unlimited potentialities for self-liberation and self-conquest. Our time summons the middle class to remember these innate powers and to take their stand upon them intellectually and ethically. The right to power is contingent upon the conviction that one has a historic mission to perform. If any class refuses to do this, or is too weak, it will have to step aside, abdicate power, and make way for a type that knows none of the inhibitions and ties of atavistic sentiment, which, one cannot but fear at times, may render the European middle class unfit to guide the body politic and economic into a new world.
Without doubt, the credit that history is still willing to accord to the bourgeois republic to-day—a short-term credit, indeed—rests upon the faith not yet lost that democracy also has that ability which its increasingly powerful enemies claim as their own: the ability to undertake our guidance into the new age. It is not by staging celebrations for its great sons that the middle class proves itself worthy of them. The greatest of these, Goethe, hails it:
Turn your backs upon dead trappings,
Let us love what is alive!
Whose words are these? We are in the spring of 1932. The themes are familiar. The appeal to the educated middle class standing at a turning point. The idea of living on borrowed time.
The obvious suspect is John Maynard Keynes. And yet this is clearly not Keynes. For one, if this passage was by Keynes, it would be very well-known. But it is also a little too bombastic, too European in its evocation of class categories and the reference to Goethe would be out of character too.
In fact, it is the text of a speech written by Thomas Mann speaking on the centennial of the death of his great literary hero Goethe on March 22, 1932.
Nevertheless, the resemblance in contemporary diagnosis between Keynes and Mann is intriguing. In continuation of the thought begun in Chartbook 463, it is fascinating to explore the parallels and divergences between two of the most famous liberal intellectuals of the period from the 1920s to the 1940s.

-
-
Was there contact between them? Not, as far as we know, in direct terms. So what follows is not intellectual history but speculative juxtaposition. Nevertheless, the connection is not merely imaginary.
Mann can hardly have not known about Keynes. No educated German could have been ignorant of The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919). Indeed Mann’s diary records him reading excerpts from the book in February 1920 and delighting at the portrayal of Wilson. As one would expect, Mann invokes “Keynes’s book” as a household term.

-
- Conversely, after the critical success of Buddenbrooks (1901) and The Magic Mountain (1924), the Bloomsbury group must surely have had views about Mann, who went on to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929.
And yet there is no evidence that Keynes ever read Thomas Mann. He was far more interested in Ibsen plays and Russian ballet than contemporary continental novels. It is a remarkable and perhaps telling missed connection, one that points to the relatively hermetic nature of much of middle class culture, particularly in early twentieth-century Britain.
After all, their preoccupations were deeply aligned.
Both were fundamentally interested in the fate but also the role and responsibility of the social elites inherited from the nineteenth century in the twentieth century.
Keynes’s opening to the Economic Consequences of the Peace could have come straight out of a Mann novel, except that in Mann it would have been tongue in cheek.
As Mann himself later remarked in a talk at Princeton given in 1939, Zauberberg, his great novel looking back at bourgeois life in the pre-1914 period, was only imaginable under conditions of “intact” capitalism.
For Keynes, the underlying stakes were nothing less than “civilization,” a term loaded with promise and anxiety. The force of The Economic Consequences of the Peace had after all come from treating the pre-war European order as an astonishing and fragile achievement.
In “My Early Beliefs,” the memoir Keynes read to his Bloomsbury friends in September 1938 in the midst of the Sudeten crisis, Keynes looked back on the confident rationalism of his pre-war youth and judged it “disastrously mistaken.” What he and his friends had missed was the existence of “irrational springs of wickedness in most men.” “We were not aware that civilisation was a thin and precarious crust erected by the personality and the will of a very few, and only maintained by rules and conventions skilfully put across and guilefully preserved.” It is this startling confession about the precarity of civilization that underpins Keynes’s quest for renewal and reinvention.
For the young Mann, by contrast, the same term was very nearly a slur. During World War I, and then most explicitly in his Reflections of a Nonpolitical Man (1918), he had built a whole metaphysics out of pitting “civilization” against Kultur. Civilization was the shallow, sociable, rationalizing West: epitomized by the Enlightenment, France, democracy, “literature,” even politics as such. Kultur, by contrast, was a peculiarly German thing: arising from the soul, endowed with depth, and expressed in music, form, art, indeed in the daemonic. “The difference between Geist and politics,” Mann wrote, “contains that between culture and civilization, between soul and society, between freedom and the franchise, between art and literature.” Culture was where the enchantment lived.
Having drawn this map in which enlightenment rationalism was neatly separated from the magical realm culture, within a few years he redrew it.
Already by the early 1920s Mann had dissolved the binary. In his extraordinary speech “Von deutscher Republik” (On the German Republic) given in October 1922, which startled his admirers on the right, Mann declared himself for the Weimar Republic and simultaneously insisted this was no mere recantation of his earlier beliefs. Instead, he announced by way of the unlikely duo of Novalis and Whitman “the identity of humanity and democracy,” the first being “only a classicistically old-fashioned name for the second.” Kultur and civilization, the German romantic and the American democrat. The antitheses on which his wartime Reflections had rested were now to be reconciled through the republican state and under the heading of humanity. By 1932, summoning the bourgeoisie to “guide” society into a rational new order, Mann speaks in almost exactly the civilizational register the author of the Reflections had ridiculed. That intellectual and political migration is what lets Mann’s Goethe speech begin to sound like Keynes.
By the early 1930s, theirs was thus a shared question: How do we make modern civilization work under conditions that are both affluent and yet fraught?
Like Mann, Keynes had a deep sense of inherited ideas as both powerful and out of step with the world. The profound sense that the old order was taking itself down to ruin and had to be reinvented in order to be saved, is common to both of them.
Both of them were reluctant but realistic exponents of modern democracy.
The working class as the unexpected but essential ally against bourgeois philistinism, in favor of modern intellectual and cultural progress – Mann and Keynes also agree on this.
Most fundamentally, both situated their contemporary interventions and historical reflections within a historical schema of transition.
Mann’s 1932 Goethe speech was the warrant for Georg Lukács’s claim that Mann was the “last great critical realist”. Like the modernists of his generation – Woolf, Joyce, Proust – Mann was caught up in the exploration of inner life. Under conditions of late capitalism, Lukács argued, nothing else was possible. But unlike his contemporaries, Mann remained rooted in a broader, overarching view of history, precisely the socio-economic trajectory set out in his Goethe speech: towards “(t)he new, socialized world, the world of planning and co-operation”. This meant that Mann’s Zauberberg (as argued in the last Chartbook 463) is not just a case study of subjective disorientation, but truly a structural account of the drifting apart of subjective time and objective history. This was for Lukács (and for Adorno’s btw) the essential hallmark of “realism” under conditions of late capitalism.
Taking up the Lukácsian reading, would it be too far-fetched to suggest that Keynes, in his own domain, was accomplishing something similar?
If Mann (as read by Lukács) was the last great critical realist because he accounted in grand architecture of his novels for the disintegration of the classic unity of subjective time and objective historical development, was Keynes, in his General Theory (1936), not trying to do something similar for the domain of political economy? Was Keynes not corralling the dispersed fragments of a late-nineteenth-century coherence into a new and more general framework, an intervention that was both radical and at the same time an act of preservation, not to say conservation?
Keynes’s basic diagnosis was that the old properties of a well-functioning market economy and with it the self-confident subjectivity of bourgeois identity, consumption, and personal freedom were no longer in evidence. Conservatives might insist that the only way forward was a hard-faced return to the nineteenth century. But for Keynes that amounted to a form of denial. The other great experiments of the age, the new model of 1920s Soviet civilization, as well as the distasteful centralized authoritarian regimes of Italian fascism and German Nazism, were at least able to reckon with the rupture.
But liberalism had no reason to abandon itself to this bad set of choices. If it actually occupied the space of sex-life-death – i.e. biopolitics, Mann’s preeminent domain – and at the same time situated its economic policy within an enlightened macroeconomics, framed not as a “special” case but by a “general theory” – what Mann’s novels did in narrative terms – liberalism could regain its agency and vindicate the special role of the educated elite as guiding all of society into a better and more civilized future. As both Mann and Keynes insisted, liberalism need not be shy, it need not concede the future to the fascists, so long as it put itself on the historical front foot. It must demonstrate its capacity to “guide”, as Mann put it in his Goethe speech.
That also meant accounting for one’s own vantage point in addressing a bourgeois audience. Like Keynes, Mann inhabited the contradictions of this bourgeois perspective with preternatural ease, as Lukács already observed in his essay “In Search of Bourgeois Man,” written in 1945 in honour of Mann’s seventieth birthday. Describing Mann as “the last great bourgeois writer,” Lukács highlighted his “dialectically complex attitude to the middle class.”
If we think of economics and the novel as two distinctively modern “technologies” of sense-making in bourgeois society, and if those apparatuses first took on their consolidated “classic” shape for the first time in the early nineteenth century, then both Mann and Keynes found ways to update and translate those technologies into the Age of Extremes. So, Keynes’s macroeconomic stands in relation to its Marshallian forebears, as, according to Lukács, Mann’s novels stand in relation to their nineteenth-century predecessors.
But if this parallelism is illuminating there is another deeper motif that it may unlock.
What, after all, is the pivot we are using for this speculative exercise? A speech commemorating the dominant figure of modern German culture, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749-1832).
For Mann’s sense of history (and for Lukács’s reading of Mann as a historical thinker and writer) it is not just the crisis of World War I that is key. It is not by accident that in the midst of the crisis, in 1932, Mann should return to Goethe as his essential anchor point, straddling the Sattelzeit (Koselleck) between the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Furthermore, by way of Goethe’s own historical vista, Mann opens to the seventeenth century and the age of alchemy supposedly overcome by enlightenment rationalism. Hence the figure of Dr Faustus.
Geoff Mann (no relation) has recently given us a brilliantly illuminating reading of Keynesianism, also in terms of the Sattelzeit, but in his case by way of Hegel. This is inspired less by any specific indebtedness of Keynes to Hegel, than by Geoff Mann’s productive wrestling with Marxist readings of Keynes – above all that of Toni Negri.
In rewriting Keynes as the theorists of the thermidor, Geoff Mann gives us a tour de force in every sense of that phrase.
Our reading of Keynes in light of Thomas Mann suggests an alternative, less conservative, speculative history. On our reading, the historical depth to Mann and Keynes’s liberalism would be provided not by Hegel and his visions of the state, but by figures of bourgeois genius like Goethe and, on Keynes’s side, his great heroes of the seventeenth and early eighteenth century.
Thomas Mann’s reading of the late Goethe is worth quoting at length:

> This bold, dream-like anticipation of a new society to succeed the bourgeois order is as remarkable, as impressive, as the old man’s growing interest in engineering projects of utopian scope, his enthusiasm for undertakings like the cutting through of the Isthmus of Panama. He talks of these things insistently and goes into detail as if they were of more importance to him than all the poetry in the world, and that is true, in the last analysis. His optimistic delight in the scientific side of civilization, affecting communications particularly, need cause no surprise in view of the end of Faust, who experiences his highest moment in the realization of a utilitarian dream, the draining of a swamp—a peculiar affront, indeed, to the one-sidedly aesthetic and philosophical trend of the age! In the same way, Goethe was astonishingly indefatigable in his old age in discussing the possibilities of joining the Gulf of Mexico with the Pacific, and in expatiating on the incalculable effects of such a feat upon the whole world, civilized and uncivilized alike. He wanted the United States to undertake the work, and his fancy dwells upon the prosperous cities that would spring up one after another along the Pacific coast, where nature had so felicitously prepared the ground for man by making good harbors. He could hardly wait for that to come about—that and the joining of the Danube and the Rhine, a perfectly staggering project, to be sure, along with a third very great project, the Suez Canal for the English. “To see all that,” he exclaims, “might make it worth while to hold out on this earth for another fifty years.” He cast his eyes over the earth, refusing to stop short at the borders of his own country; his enthusiasm for the future was vast enough to take in the whole world; and the quickening of life, the joys and sorrows, of foreign nations affected him as did those of his own people. His was an imperialism of love—the imperialism of an august mind risen above barriers of nationality, a mind that cherished liberty particularly under its aspect of greatness. It is the same trait that we have already seen in his heralding of a world literature. In setting itself to create a utopia of applied science, the bourgeois outlook expands to world-wide proportions; it turns into “communism,” taking that word in a sufficiently broad, undogmatic sense. This is an enthusiasm of a sober sort. But what we need to-day is the sobering of a world that is dying from the strangle-hold of emotional survivals. Who was it who said that the Germans should be prohibited from using the word “Gemüt” for fifty years? It was Germany’s greatest poet. The middle-class man is lost and is doomed to be swept aside in the era that is approaching unless he can succeed in ridding himself of the fatal sentiment and life-sapping principles that still govern his thinking. He must bravely espouse the future. It is idle to scorn reason and hold to a stubborn cult of atavistic feeling which, in present conditions, appears utterly blind and senseless—a kind of desperate, malignant, murderous sentimentalism.
It is as though Thomas Mann is reading Goethe by way of Keynes’s “Economic Possibilities of our Grandchildren”, which had been published in June 1930.
Which suggests the question – riffing this time on Geoff Mann rather than Thomas Mann – are all true Keynesians not so much descendants of Hegelian, as children of Goethe?
A textbook description of the Weimar classicism shaped by Goethe and Schiller in the transition from the eighteenth to the nineteenth century, would describe it as the synthesis of rationalism of the Enlightenment with the romantic, “animal spirits” of Sturm und Drang, a decidedly “Keynesian” formulation. An argument for Goethe over Hegel could be made simply on grounds of precedence and preeminence. By the late eighteenth century, Goethe was a cultural star of quite different proportions than Hegel. Whereas Hegel was an awed spectator of Napoleonic history, Goethe was on the young Bonaparte’s bedside table. As Emperor, Napoleon received Goethe for a personal audience in October 1808. Indeed, as Napoleonic historian Nicolas Broussard remarks:

> Hegel opens his lessons on Roman history by reporting the famous bit of conversation between Goethe and Napoleon: “One day he was conversing with Goethe about the nature of tragedy. He expressed then the opinion that the modern tragedy was differing from the old one essentially in that we do not have fate any more of which men will succumb and that in the place of the ancient Fatum has appeared politics. It should thus be used as the modern destiny for tragedy, as the power of circumstances to which the individual has to bend to.” (Lectures, p.215).
Once again this is a chain of intellectual association without textual warrant in Keynes himself. The point of making it is to answer Geoff Mann’s brilliant Marxo-Hegelian reading by way of Negri with one derived from Thomas Mann by way of Georg Lukács.
Keynes, himself, might very well have been bewildered by either chain of association. After all, he situated himself self-consciously in the tradition of English political thought that descended from Hobbes and Locke. His most charged points of identification lay with figures the “nineteenth century” had flattened and which Keynes set about disinterring.
The first was Thomas Robert Malthus, almost exactly Goethe’s contemporary and, in Keynes’s insistent phrase, “the first of the Cambridge economists.” What Keynes prized in Malthus was precisely what the nineteenth century had discarded. Malthus was the road modern political economy had failed to take, defeated and buried by Ricardo. For the discipline had refused to build on Malthus the “inductive and intuitive investigator,” the mind that stayed close to the texture of experience. Instead, Ricardo’s more abstract intellectual constructions proved victorious. The triumph of the cleaner, colder system produced a science remade in the misleading image of purified reason. Keynes presented his own task as revealing why the subsequent century of Ricardian dominance had been a “disaster,” stuck in an “artificial groove.”
To recover Malthus was to reopen the groove, to insist that the ancestor the nineteenth century had buried was the richer mind who had come to economic questions “by the best of all routes,” beginning as a philosopher and moral scientist, passing through history, and only then arriving at theory, as Keynes put it the biographical essay he finally published in 1933 he made the stakes plain. To describe that arrival Keynes reached for a startling image of transformation: “from being a caterpillar of a moral scientist and a chrysalis of an historian, he could at last spread the wings of his thought and survey the world as an economist.” It is an image of magic and metamorphosis: a shapeshifting creature that leaps from one fixed form into another, unrecognisable and more alive.
This was exactly the image Keynes would reach for again, on a far grander scale, when he turned from Malthus to a stranger and even more charismatic ancestor, reaching back past the eighteenth century into the seventeenth: Isaac Newton.
In 1936, Keynes, a long admirer of Newton, purchased the scientists’ unpublished manuscripts at a Sotheby auction. He reportedly paid £3,000 or around £200,000 today adjusted for inflation. As Keynes was surprised to discover, the manuscripts he had purchased reflected Newton’s extensive interest in the subject of alchemy. By Keynes’s own estimation, Newton scribbled perhaps a million words in notes on alchemical matters. As Keynes came to realize, Newton was not just the first of the scientists, but the last of the magicians.
In the remarkable commemorative essay that he penned for December 1942 the anniversary of Newton’s birth, Keynes started by apologizing for the fact that “The war has deprived me both of leisure to treat adequately so great a theme and of opportunity to consult my library and my papers and to verify my impressions … .” He then went on:

> “I believe that Newton was different from the conventional picture of him. But I do not believe he was less great. He was less ordinary, more extraordinary, than the nineteenth century cared to make him out. Geniuses are very peculiar. Let no one here suppose that my object today is to lessen, by describing, Cambridge’s greatest son. I am trying rather to see him as his own friends and contemporaries saw him. And they without exception regarded him as one of the greatest of men. In the eighteenth century and since, Newton came to be thought of as the first and greatest of the modern age of scientists, a rationalist, one who taught us to think on the lines of cold and untinctured reason. I do not see him in this light. I do not think that any one who has pored over the contents of that box which he packed up when he finally left Cambridge in 1696 and which, though partly dispersed, have come down to us, can see him like that. Newton was not the first of the age of reason. He was the last of the magicians, the last of the Babylonians and Sumerians, the last great mind which looked out on the visible and intellectual world with the same eyes as those who began to build our intellectual inheritance rather less than 10,000 years ago. Isaac Newton, a posthumous child born with no father on Christmas Day, 1642, was the last wonderchild to whom the Magi could do sincere and appropriate homage.”
What is extraordinary about this essay, as about Thomas Mann’s rereading of Goethe in 1932, is its historical creativity. Keynes summons a new Newton, one freed from the encrustations of the nineteenth century. One that is both stranger and yet also more alive, freed from the wax works and thus present in the twentieth century. As one contemporary remarked, Keynes described Newton as “Copernicus and Faustus in one, and doubtless he thought he resembled them both”.
Ultimately, this is what makes Keynes and Mann kindred spirits: the ambition not only to rethink the position of the twentieth-century bourgeoisie, and its politics of liberalism in relation to the tensions of their moment, but also to give that politics a new history in the grandest sense.
I love putting out Chartbook. I am particularly pleased that it goes out for free to thousands of subscribers around the world. But, writing this newsletter takes a lot of work. reads.title: An overview of Gamma Exposure and GEX tools
reads.subtitle: Gamma Exposure Simplified
reads.body:
In this article, snorlax_uw will quickly go over GAMMA EXPOSURE as a concept as well as quickly touch on several of the different GEX tools available to you.

## GEX Theory
Gamma exposure theory, or GEX, assumes that market makers (MMs) are the counterparty to nearly every options transaction, and that on balance they end up buying calls (from investors selling calls for income) and selling puts (to investors buying puts for downside protection).
MMs aren’t taking a directional view: their job is to provide the markets with liquidity, and the inventory they accumulate (the long calls and short puts) are a byproduct of this job: unwanted directional risk they now have to neutralize. They accomplish this buy buying or selling shares of the underlying stock.
Gamma exposure measures the estimated dollar value of the shares that MMs are estimated to need to buy or sell in the open market in order to balance their trading books as the underlying price moves by 1%.
Simply put:
When GEX is positive, dealers sell into rallies and buy into dips, which tends to dampen volatility.
When it’s negative, they do the opposite — buying strength and selling weakness — which amplifies moves.

## GEX Methodologies, Ranked (best to worst)
GEX has become increasingly popular in the options space. There are several methodologies used to output GEX data, all of which are available on Unusual Whales. I’ll list them out here, ranked by how clear the signal is from best to worst.
After you read the top ranked view (item 1, Periscope) I’d actually suggest going to item 4 (open interest), then reading 3 (intraday volume) and then 2 (intraday volume, with bid/ask side attribution) as views 2-4 build on top of their respective predecessor.

## 1) Periscope SPX MM GEX
The Periscope GEX data (only available for ticker SPX) runs on a dataset provided DIRECTLY FROM CBOE. A 10-minute refresh (Retail Pro subscription) and a 1-minute refresh (Retail Max) are available: view our plans.
SPX options are EXCLUSIVE to CBOE, unlike a ticker such as SPY which trades across over a dozen different options exchanges.
The exclusivity of SPX to CBOE provides Unusual Whales with a direct-line to the ACTUAL buy/sell data.
EVERY OTHER GEX TOOL ON THE INTERNET THAT DOES NOT USE THIS CBOE DATA, including other tools available on Unusual Whales that you will read about below, operate based on assumptions (raw volume or raw open interest). Periscope makes no such assumptions, as it knows EXACTLY what is being bought/sold and by whom.
Another feature that sets this CBOE dataset apart is that it also differentiates between customer and MM orders and ONLY returns data on MM positioning, further cutting through much of the noise that exists with other GEX tools.
Periscope is one of the most used tools on Unusual Whales, and rightly so.

-
-

## 2) Intraday Volume, with bid/ask side attribution
The methodology in item 3, Intraday Volume, can further be enhanced by adding ‘side’ attribution data. https://unusualwhales.com/stock/SPY/greek-exposure?tab=Spot (select Directionalized Volume using the dropdown)
This methodology adds additional color to the by considering the bid/ask/fill relationship of every transaction.
It infers that trades at or closer to the ask were bought by customers, and trades at or closer to the bid were sold by customers.
This is a meaningful improvement from methodologies 3 and 4, but still flawed because it still makes assumptions.

-
- By the time you’re reading this we will likely have released a heatmap style view of this data that has recently become popularized.

-
-

## 3) Intraday Volume
GEX methodologies that use intraday options volume are a step up from the ‘open interest’ based GEX. https://unusualwhales.com/stock/SPY/greek-exposure?tab=Spot (select Total Volume using the dropdown)
This methodology swaps the stale open interest data with something slightly better (albeit still flawed in its own right): raw intraday trading volumes.
This view assumes that dealers are long all calls and short all puts traded.
Any kind of assumption in GEX is inherently flawed, and volume based GEX is no exception. Consider that a call contract opened and closed in the same session results in no net position, but this type of methodology would effectively count this round trip as 2 that the MMs must now hedge for.

-
-

## 4) Open Interest
The classic ‘GEX’ view uses options open interest data provided daily by the OCC (options clearing corporation) to return exposure data.
This view assumes that dealers are long all calls and short all puts in open interest.
As open interest only updates once per session in the premarket this data can be seen as stale.
This is by far the simplest, and perhaps fitting, least accurate type of GEX view.

reads.title: War Is Dangerous, but Miscalculation Is What Makes It Go Global. Here Is How This War Goes Global.
reads.subtitle: The danger is not that the players are reckless. The danger is that they are all being careful, and careful still ends in catastrophe when everyone is reading a different map.
reads.body:
Let me say the thing about this war that actually keeps me up, because it is not the thing most people fear. The common worry is that someone reckless will do something insane and blow the Middle East region or even Europe apart. That is not what worries me. What worries me is the opposite. Everyone at this table is being careful. Every actor is calculating, hedging, trying to stay inside the lines. And careful, calculating, disciplined actors can still walk a region straight into a global war, because carefulness offers NO protection at all when each side is being careful according to a different map. The catastrophe does not require a madman. It only requires that two rational men are each certain about a line that is not where they think it is.
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

> Why regional wars go global
Here is the mechanism, stated as plainly as I can. A regional war stays regional for exactly as long as every major actor correctly reads three things about every other actor: their red lines, their capacity, and their resolve. Where the line is that must not be crossed. Whether the other side actually has the means it appears to have. And whether it possesses the will to use them.
Get all three right, on every axis, and you can fight a contained, brutal, terrible war that stays inside its box for years. Get any one of them wrong, and the box breaks, and the actors who were never in the regional fight are suddenly dragged into a global one.
That is NOT a theory. It is the entire history of how wars go global, compressed into a single variable. Let me show you the record.
Share
Leave a comment

- 1914 was not chosen by anyone. No European leader in July of that year wanted the four-year industrial slaughter that followed. What they wanted was a short, sharp, contained war won by Christmas, and every one of them miscalculated how the alliance system behind their opponent would move. Each read the others’ resolve wrong. Each assumed the other would back down or stay out. The war did not come from a decision to go big. It came from a cascade of leaders who each decided to go small and each misjudged the response.

-
-
- Korea went global on a single misread of a red line. When UN forces drove north toward the Yalu, the assumption in command was that China would not intervene, would not cross the river, did not have the resolve or would not take the risk. Beijing had signalled otherwise. The signal was not believed. Hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops crossed, and a contained war became a different and far larger one, because one commander was certain about a line that was not where he thought it was.

-
- Look across every catastrophic expansion in modern history and the pattern holds. The war did not widen because someone chose to widen it. It widened because someone miscalculated how the other side would respond to a limited move. The escalation was never the plan. It was the price of an error about someone else’s mind.

> The operational anatomy of a misread
Now let me make this operational, because “miscalculation” is a soft word for a set of hard, specific mechanisms, and naming them is how you learn to watch for them.

- The first is the capacity misread. This is misjudging what the other side actually has, as opposed to what it displays. Every military maintains a gap between its real magazine and its theatrical one, deliberately, because deterrence runs on perceived capability. The danger is that you come to believe your adversary’s bluff is real and freeze, or, far worse, you come to believe his real capability is a bluff and act. Both are capacity misreads, and the second one starts wars.

- The second is the resolve misread, and it is the most common and most lethal. This is misjudging not what the other side can do but whether it will. Resolve is invisible. It lives inside the mind of the decision-maker under stress, and it cannot be measured from outside, only inferred, which means it is guessed. Korea was a resolve misread. Most wars of expansion are. An actor concludes the other side lacks the will to respond to a limited provocation, and is wrong.
Subscribe now
Get 7 day free trial

- The third is the red-line misread. This is being certain about where the other side’s threshold sits, and being wrong about its location. Red lines are frequently ambiguous on purpose, because a state that names its exact threshold hands the adversary a map of precisely how far it can push without triggering a response. So the lines stay blurry, and the blur is where the war widens, because each side privately believes it knows where the line is, and the two private maps do not match.

- The fourth, and the one that ties them together, is the mirror-imaging error. This is the analyst’s cardinal sin: assuming the other side reasons the way you do, values what you value, and will therefore respond as you would in its position. It is the reason a Western planner misreads a civilizational strategic culture that measures time in decades and answers late by design. Mirror-imaging feels like empathy but functions as blindness, because it substitutes your own decision-making for the adversary’s, and the adversary is not you.
Every one of these is a reading of another actor’s mind, under stress, with incomplete information, on a compressed clock. That is not a war held together by wisdom. It is a war held together by four or five simultaneous guesses all staying correct at the same time.

> Where the misreads live right now
So look at this theatre and count them, because they are all live, all at once.
Iran is reading how much of America’s magazine is real versus theatre, how many munitions, how much sustained appetite, how much of the pressure is genuine capacity and how much is performance for a domestic audience.
A capacity misread in either direction is dangerous. If Tehran overestimates American staying power it may concede ground it did not need to. If it underestimates it, it may reach for the chokepoint believing Washington cannot sustain the response, and be wrong.
Israel is reading how far it can strike before its patron is forced to choose. That is a red-line misread waiting to happen, because the American threshold, how much Israeli action Washington will absorb before it has to either fully commit or visibly restrain its ally, is genuinely ambiguous, and Israel is navigating by a private estimate of a line the Americans have deliberately left blurry.
Washington is reading how much pressure Tehran absorbs before it reaches for the strait instead of the table. That is a resolve misread in the making, because it depends entirely on a judgment about Iranian will under siege, and Iranian will is precisely the variable that Western analysis has misjudged repeatedly, because it keeps mirror-imaging a patience it reads as weakness.
And behind Iran sit two great powers, Russia and China, each reading whether its own credibility now requires it to move. This is the most dangerous reading of all, because it is recursive: Moscow and Beijing are not just calculating the regional war, they are calculating what their inaction signals to every other client and adversary watching. A point may arrive where a great power concludes that staying out costs more in credibility than coming in costs in risk. That calculation is where a regional war acquires its third and fourth participants.
Every one of those is a guess about another actor’s mind. The war is being held together, right now, by all of them staying correct simultaneously. The moment one breaks, the box breaks with it.

> Why this is worse than recklessness
Here is the part that inverts the usual fear, and it is the core of the strategic-realism read. We instinctively look for the villain, the reckless actor who wants the wider war, because a villain is legible and can be deterred or removed. But the historical record says the wider war almost never comes from the actor who wants it. It comes from the careful actor who has misjudged the board and does not yet know it.
This is why recklessness is, perversely, less dangerous than confident error. A reckless actor announces himself and can be contained. A careful, rational, disciplined actor operating on a wrong map gives no warning, because from the inside his error feels exactly like sound judgment. He is not gambling. He is certain. And certainty built on a misread is the most dangerous condition in strategy, because it removes the very caution that might otherwise save the situation. The man who thinks he might be wrong hedges. The man who is certain he is right commits. And the second man, when his certainty is misplaced, is the one who breaks the box.
Subscribe now
Get 7 day free trial
The most dangerous sentence in any war room is not “let us escalate.” Escalation, spoken aloud, is a decision that can be debated, resisted, walked back. The most dangerous sentence is “they would never.” Because “they would never” is not a decision. It is an assumption, usually unexamined, often unspoken, that sits underneath the plan and is never stress-tested until it fails. They would never cross the Yalu. They would never let the alliance drag them in. They would never absorb that strike without folding. Every one of those sentences preceded a catastrophe, and every one felt like realism to the person who thought it.

reads.title: Wrong War, Wrong Century
reads.subtitle: 20th Century Warfare Attacked the 21st
reads.body:
The American MIC put together an unbeatable military machine, at least when it comes to blasting the ever-loving shit out of 2nd and 3rd tier countries that can’t really fight back. I call it the “Top Gun Maverick Military Model.”

-
- The TGM3 works great in C.G. Hollywood movies, it worked great in the 20th Century against countries like Serbia and Libya, and most importantly of all, it’s fantastic for shoveling endless billions of dollars to our corpulent MIC “defense” industries. And for decades, it kept the rest of the world in line, afraid to test America’s evidently overwhelming destructive military power.
That is, until President Donald Trump, tricked by Bibi Netanyahu’s false promise of a quick and easy three-day regime-change victory over Iran, blundered into the greatest military disaster in modern history--and thereby exposed the obsolescence of the TGM3 against the 21st-Century Modern Missile Model, or the 21CM3. [I’m making up silly acronyms on the fly, so that the Internet Military Analysts’ Union will take me seriously.]
If the USAF and the IDF/AF launch another massive air blitz on Iran, as Trump threatened a few days ago, the key battle equation will be USAF air tankers vs. Iranian MRBMs, as seen below.

-
- Not directly, of course, but the Iranian missiles can be used to destroy USAF tankers on the ground before they can take off to refuel the USAF and IDF/AF attack planes. This will give Iran the opportunity to spoil any such US-Israel air blitz before it can reach its crescendo.
Iran will not strike first, out of the blue, preemptively, but they will wait until they can see (from Russian and Chinese satellite intelligence, and from agents on the ground), that the main force is launching into the air. When some percentage of the air armada is airborne, say 30 or 40%, Iran will launch a furious missile attack on the air bases indicated on the below map, (and on other bases I don’t know about, but Iran surely does.)
If runways are cratered or even pitted, takeoffs can be aborted, and airborne jets will have to find alternate landing strips. This will upset the careful timing of the air blitz, since returning aircraft will be unable to return to their launching airfields to refuel and rearm and take off for their next scheduled sortie.
Timing is the crucial element in such an air blitz, and in Iran’s counter-attack using MRBMs. The Khorramshahr 4 missile with 80 submunitions seems to me as if it was designed for exactly this scenario. It was demonstrated in Tel Aviv last March, but has not been used since (that I know of). 80 bomblets are sufficient to heavily damage jet aircraft parked close together on concrete aprons, as well as to pit the runways, creating potholes and “FOD,” or foreign object debris, which must be cleaned up for the runway to be put back into full use.
Even if the runways are put out of action for a matter of only hours, this is enough time to spoil the carefully choreographed timing of a major air blitz on Iran. And any aircraft damaged on the ground will not be able to take part in the attack at all.
Planes which were in the air when the missile counter-strike took place, which are forced to land at alternate runways, will not be able to rearm and rejoin the air battle during the compressed window while it’s underway.

-
- A few days ago, a drone struck an LNG vessel docked in Egypt called a the “Energos Winter,” one of a class of FSRUs, or Floating Storage and Regasification Units. Most folks have confused this with an LNG tanker, this is partly but not completely correct. I asked Grok to explain the distinction:

-
- GROK: What was the LNG platform that was struck in Damietta Egypt a few days ago? A tanker ship the propels itself from port to port, or a stationary floating LNG liquefaction and gasification facility?
“The Energos Winter was functioning in the FSRU import role when hit. The vessel struck was the Energos Winter, a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU). It is a self-propelled tanker-style ship (capable of sailing between ports under its own power) that was moored and operating as Egypt’s floating import terminal at Damietta. A secondary LNG carrier, Gaslog Salem, was also affected. It is not a stationary liquefaction facility.”

-
- The important point here is that Damietta, where the Energos Winter was hit by a drone, is 50 KM to the west of Port Said and the top of the Suez Canal. If the missile came from Iran, it flew low and slow over the canal and many built up urban areas on its route. If it was launched by the Houthis, it flew the length of the canal.
This drone strike was merely a warning shot. The drone was only meant to start a fire in the superstructure. These LNG facilities are crammed with fire-fighting systems for obvious reasons. The fire was put out.
BUT, if the Iranians fired an MRBM with a 1,500 kg warhead, striking the Energos Winter at hypersonic speed would have caused a massive catastrophe. These FSRUs feed natural gas to Egypt. Beside the immediate local disaster, Iran’s gas system could be crippled. Factories would close, and electrical power plants would go off line.
Or, an Iranian MRBM could hit an American ship in the Suez Canal itself.  Its warhead, striking at hypersonic speed, would not only sink the ship, it would likely blow it apart. In 2021 the Ever Given container ship blocked the canal for a week after simply going aground, fully intact. If ships are shattered and sunk in the canal, it could be blocked indefinitely. A reminder: the Suez Canal was blocked for 7 years following the 1967 “Six Day War,” a so-called “preemptive” war begun by Israel with sneak-attacks against Egypt and Syria.

-
-

## How War Marooned 15 Ships in The Suez Canal For Eight Years

-
- Another interesting aspect of the current war is that drones like the one that struck the LNG facility in Egypt are a near-perfect false-flag weapon. Unlike ballistic missiles, they can  be programmed to attack from any direction, after taking routes designed to conceal their origin. We have seen this constantly in the Ukraine war, with drones programmed to strike from directions that will minimize their exposure to air defenses. We are assuming that Iran or the Houthis fired the drone at Damietta, it can’t be ruled out that this was a false-flag attack by Israel, designed to widen the war. This is unlikely in this particular case, but it’s something to keep in mind when regarding drone attacks.
And don’t rule out home-built American drones being used to attack refineries and chemical plants in the United States. The plans are now open source, and any skilled hobbyist capable of building a race car, a speedboat or a kit airplane can build a Shahed-type drone in a garage workshop. We will see them in the coming years.

-
- Now, if anyone is wondering who is winning or losing the war that Donald Trump began on February 28, with sneak-attack assassination missile strikes during negotiations, here is a handy score card. The nation that is abandoning bases and moving away from its enemy is the side that is losing. We have abandoned 5th Fleet HQ in Bahrain, and we are leaving our bases in Kuwait and Iraq, among others. They are too close to Iran to be protected by our dwindling stock of interceptor missiles.

-
- Another clear metric for determining the outcome of this war is to ask, who is in control of the Strait of Hormuz? The US Navy had dominated the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman since the 1940s, and now it has been driven out of the region.

-
- Yes, the US Navy can still put a secondary blockade on ships leaving the Persian Gulf, but this doesn’t solve our problems, it only creates more, as this outrageously stupid war of choice drives the global economy into a great depression and possible famine. This will correctly be blamed on Trump and the United States, and it may well mark the end of the US dollar as the world reserve currency, as nations dump our Treasuries and move toward the BRICs and other more reliable financial arrangements.
It has also exposed the American military as an obsolete 20th Century museum relic, which cannot even force its will on 2nd-tier Iran, much less upon Russia or China. So while our own economy crumbles, we will no longer be able to force other nations to dance to our tune under the twin threats of economic sanctions and military action.
And this was all an entirely self-inflicted wound.

-
- Also, I just appeared on Dialogue Works with Nima Alkhorshid, discussing current developments in the Iran war, the greatest blunder in modern military history.

-
-

reads.title: Ceuta: Did Israel and US engineer the crisis?
reads.subtitle: Israel and the US exploited the Ceuta crisis. But did their involvement go further?
reads.body:
- Last Thursday and Friday, around 60,000 people crossed from Morocco into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, almost doubling its population. Many of them swam. At least 72 died in the attempt.
Almost all have since returned to Morocco. But the episode provoked a major crisis for Spain’s government. Other European countries turned on Madrid, claiming that its migration policy was responsible. Italy’s hard-right government temporarily reintroduced border controls on arrivals from Spain.
The far right across Europe and the wider West was jubilant. Here, they claimed, was proof of their narrative about a migrant invasion of Europe – and of the supposedly inevitable consequences of Spain’s progressive government taking a more humane approach to migration.
Help us take on the Establishment media by becoming a free or paid subscriber.

## The far right seizes the crisis
Spain’s far-right Vox party called the crossings an “invasion”, demanded the complete closure of the border and linked the migrants to sexual violence and stabbings. Vox could be in government next year through a coalition with the hard-right People’s Party.
Donald Trump similarly declared that the crossings “look like an invasion”, before turning the deaths and desperation in Ceuta into a campaign message:

> “That same thing’s going to happen to us if the Republicans don’t get elected, except worse.”
The US State Department went further:

> “This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe.
“We are considering actions to defend Americans at home and abroad from this threat and stand ready to assist other European allies considering similar options.”
Vice-President JD Vance posted:

> “Thank God @POTUS was elected and our country’s border no longer looks like this.
“These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West.”
Nigel Farage, the leader of Britain’s hard-right Reform UK, declared: “This is battle for the future of our civilisation.”
Other Reform politicians joined in. Suella Braverman claimed: “Make no mistake, these men are on their way to the UK right now.”
This was totally false. Almost all of the migrants have already been returned to Morocco.
Before turning to what actually happened – and to what could suggest possible Israeli and American involvement – it is worth challenging the claim that Spain somehow brought this crisis on itself through its migration policy.
Share

## Spain did not cause this crisis
Pedro Sánchez’s government has introduced a regularisation programme under which undocumented migrants can apply for one-year residence and work permits, provided they had lived continuously in Spain for at least five months before 1 January 2026.
The purpose was straightforward: to bring migrant workers out of the shadow economy and into legal employment, where they could pay taxes, exercise basic rights and play a full part in Spanish society.
Unlike so many other European leaders, Sánchez was prepared to tell people the truth. Welcoming migrants, he has previously said, was “an essential step to guarantee the prosperity and sustainability of our welfare state”.
But the regularisation programme had nothing to do with those attempting to enter Ceuta. None of them qualified for it.
Italian politicians and others across Europe claimed that Spain’s policy would unleash a new wave of migration into their own countries. That was simply false. The permits applied only to residence and employment in Spain. They did not grant the right to work elsewhere in Europe.
Nor did reaching Ceuta provide an automatic route to the Spanish mainland. Those crossing the border would still face extensive further legal and physical barriers before they could travel across the Strait of Gibraltar.
The politicians pretending otherwise were not confused. They were cynically exploiting public ignorance about how the system works – and the hostility towards migrants that such ignorance can so easily be used to inflame.
It is true that Spain’s Supreme Court – acting independently of the government – had ruled that people arriving by water could not be subjected to the exceptional “hot return” policy used at land fences.
But it did not prevent Spain from returning migrants. In practice, it offered those crossing into Ceuta no right to remain in Spain. But Spanish intelligence believes that people smugglers did exploit a distorted interpretation of the ruling.
Subscribe now

## Morocco let it happen
There is very strong evidence that the Moroccan state played a decisive role in this crisis.
Back in May 2021, 8,000 Moroccan migrants entered Ceuta over two days. On that occasion, Morocco had been antagonised by Spain admitting the leader of a pro-independence Western Saharan movement for medical treatment.
Western Sahara is under Moroccan occupation, and there is a powerful movement for independence. As the think tank Chatham House outline:

> “Within months, Spain had abandoned its historic position on Western Sahara – supporting an independence referendum – and instead endorsed Morocco’s autonomy plan for the territory. The lesson for Rabat, perhaps, was that pressure on Spain’s enclaves works.”
This time, the supposed pretext may have been Sánchez’s visit to Morocco’s regional rival, Algeria. He was attempting to repair relations that Algeria had severed after Spain shifted towards Morocco’s position on Western Sahara. Sánchez also discussed increasing the gas supply through a pipeline that bypasses Morocco and runs directly from Algeria to Spain.
But this was an extraordinarily weak pretext for enabling such a vast movement of people and endangering so many lives. The meeting had been announced in advance, and it did not reverse Spain’s highly favourable position towards Morocco on Western Sahara.
An Associated Press photographer at the scene said Moroccan gendarmes made no attempt to intervene as thousands of people moved past their positions towards Ceuta.
El País reported the same pattern. Moroccan auxiliary forces managed the movement of the crowd while police and gendarmes stood guard. This non-intervention continued from approximately midday on Thursday until Friday morning. The newspaper described the initial inhibition as “patent”.
In other words, Morocco’s authorities maintained order while leaving the route into Ceuta open.
Only after tens of thousands had crossed did the authorities deploy tear gas, water cannon and physical force. That matters. Once Morocco’s security forces decided to stop the movement, they demonstrated that they were perfectly capable of doing so.
More devastatingly, a report published by El Español cites sources in the Guardia Civil’s general staff who claimed Spanish border-surveillance cameras identified members of Morocco’s intelligence service among those who entered Ceuta.
Those sources claim that the alleged operatives took part to supervise the movement, observe Spain’s deployment, and monitor the response of the Spanish security forces. Spain’s intelligence sources are reported to have corroborated the Guardia Civil’s identification. The paper says other such infiltrations had been detected in previous Ceuta and Melilla crises.
Another report suggests that Spanish intelligence was concerned by nearly a thousand people swimming into Ceuta in a 10-day period. They interpreted the growing pressure as a potential test from the Moroccan state.
Spanish government sources told El País that an entry on this scale would not have been possible without the passivity of Morocco’s security forces.
Spain has continued publicly to praise Morocco as an ally. But Madrid has every reason to avoid an open confrontation: it depends on Morocco for migration control, counter-terrorism cooperation and the management of the Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla.
Subscribe now

## Morocco’s alliance with Israel and the US
All of this matters because Morocco is a close ally of both Israel and the United States, with deep economic, military, intelligence and security ties to both countries.
Morocco is one of the Arab and African countries closest to the US. It’s a major non-NATO ally which buys vast quantities of US weapons and host of African Lion, AFRICOM’s largest annual military exercise. Its security services have a strong relationship with US intelligence and law enforcement. It has a free trade agreement which underpins annual goods trade worth $7.4 billion a year.
In 2020, Morocco normalised diplomatic relations with Israel. Israel gained security access and influence in North Africa, while Morocco acquired Israeli weapons and defence technology, along with expanded intelligence and cybersecurity cooperation.
In November 2021, Israel and Morocco signed a defence memorandum establishing a formal framework for intelligence cooperation, military exercises, defence-industrial collaboration, Israeli arms sales and exchanges between the two countries’ security apparatuses.
At a meeting in January, Morocco and Israel signed a joint military work plan for 2026.
None of that proves that Israel or the US was involved in the Ceuta crisis. But it establishes the context in which the crisis took place – and the states with which Morocco’s security establishment is most closely aligned.
Subscribe now

## The US connection
Donald Trump has been enraged by Spain’s opposition to the illegal war on Iran and to Israel’s genocide in Gaza. He recently demanded an end to trade with Spain, calling the country “terrible”.
In February, written testimony from a senior fellow at the neoconservative Hudson Institute to a House Foreign Affairs subcommittee stated:

> “Morocco has been using migrants to change Spanish policy, and it has succeeded.”
In March, the right-wing, pro-war commentator and former Pentagon official Michael Rubin openly called on Morocco to organise a mass civilian mobilisation against Ceuta and Melilla.
He proposed that Moroccans gather at the frontier, send bulldozers forward and enter the cities unarmed in order to raise the Moroccan flag. Rubin is a prominent figure in Washington’s pro-Israel and national-security world.
In the weeks that followed, the House Appropriations Committee published its report on the 2027 State Department funding bill. It did two striking things.
First, it directed at least $20 million in National Security Investment Programmes and another $20 million in Foreign Military Financing to Morocco.
Second, it stated that the “Spanish-administered cities of Ceuta and Melilla are located in Moroccan territory”, noted Morocco’s claim to the cities and supported State Department efforts to encourage talks over their “future status”.
The House passed the accompanying bill on 15 July by 217 votes to 209 – just 15 days before the mass crossing.
Two days before the crossing, the US Trade and Development Agency agreed to fund a $5.7 million early engineering study for an ammonia project in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara. It was the first US government financing for a private-sector project there.
At the signing ceremony, the US ambassador declared:

> “America is in the Moroccan Sahara.”
Trump’s recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara was no longer merely diplomatic. Washington was now attaching concrete rewards to it.
The US first recognised Morocco’s claim over Western Sahara in 2020, in exchange for Morocco normalising relations with Israel. The Trump administration subsequently announced initiatives intended to mobilise $5 billion in investment involving Morocco and the wider region, as well as a weapons package.
That has now increased to at least $40 million for Moroccan security and investment programmes.
Again, none of this proves that the US organised the Ceuta crossings. But the sequence is striking: growing US hostility towards Spain, open encouragement for Morocco to mobilise against the Spanish enclaves, congressional language backing Morocco’s territorial claim, increased military support and the first US financing of a private project in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara.
Subscribe now

## The Israeli connection
Prominent Israeli figures were certainly jubilant about the crisis.
Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, declared:

> “Spain, which never misses an opportunity to lecture Israel, has declared a state of emergency in Ceuta following the crisis over its immigration policy.”
Spain had not, in fact, declared any state of emergency.
Meanwhile, the far-right Israeli minister Itamar Ben-Gvir demanded that Sánchez “open the doors of Spain and grant refuge to the residents of Gaza who seek to emigrate”.
But the most important evidence concerns the online campaign that helped bring tens of thousands of people to the border.
Anonymous social-media accounts circulated a specific message: that the Spanish border was open and that people could enter without documents.
El País found that the anonymous campaign did more than claim the frontier was open. It distributed practical advice intended to help people reach and cross the border, while one of the communities promoting the journey attracted more than 20,000 followers before being closed. The original organisers have proved difficult to trace, and automated accounts may have helped spread their material.
According to El País, the original accounts largely vanished, automated amplification may have been involved and the initial trigger has still not been identified.
After the crisis exploded, the Spanish fact-checking organisation Maldita documented the rapid appearance of posts using the hashtags #FreeCeuta and #FreeMelilla from Israeli and pro-Israeli accounts.
Al Jazeera’s open-source unit conducted a broader analysis. It found dozens of known and anonymous Israel-linked or Israel-supporting accounts using almost identical framing. The same maps, phrases and hashtags appeared repeatedly.
They found that AI-generated scenes were used to exaggerate the disorder in Ceuta. Posts described the crisis as Spain’s punishment for supporting Palestine. Hananya Naftali, a former digital-media official associated with Benjamin Netanyahu, participated in the campaign.
The timing and wording were so closely aligned that the investigators regarded them as strongly suggestive of central coordination.
That does not prove that Israel was behind the original accounts. But it would be extraordinarily naive to pretend that Israel lacks either the means or the record to conduct precisely this sort of operation.
Subscribe now

## Israel has form
France’s agency for combating foreign digital interference has accused the Israeli company BlackCore of targeting elections in several countries.
These included Scotland, where hundreds of coordinated accounts bombarded John Swinney, the SNP and the Scottish government after their criticism of Israel’s assault on Gaza. Before effectively disappearing from public view after Reuters approached it, BlackCore had publicly promoted its ability to conduct sophisticated influence operations for governments and political campaigns.
Then there is Black Cube, founded by former Israeli intelligence officers and known as the “private Mossad”. It has been accused of using fake identities, bogus job offers, hidden cameras and manufactured corruption allegations against journalists, activists and pro-Palestinian politicians – including in an alleged attempt to destabilise Slovenia’s government immediately before an election.
One of Black Cube’s advisers is Giora Eiland, the former head of Israel’s national security council. Eiland has publicly advocated depriving Gaza’s population of food, water and fuel, and welcomed the spread of epidemics as a means of securing Israeli victory.
In 2023, an undercover investigation exposed another Israeli operation, Team Jorge. The group’s founder boasted to undercover reporters that his organisation had covertly intervened in dozens of elections around the world. Its technology allowed operatives to manufacture and manage elaborate digital identities across numerous platforms, complete with some of the financial and commercial accounts that would make them appear authentic.
Its software controlled thousands of fake online personas, some equipped with email accounts, credit cards, cryptocurrency wallets and carefully fabricated lives.
We also know that Israel’s government financed a covert campaign using fake social-media accounts to target American politicians with pro-Israel propaganda. Israeli Pegasus spyware has been deployed against politicians and dissidents around the world. Israel has also dramatically expanded its official propaganda budget.
So let us be precise. None of this establishes who started the Ceuta campaign.
But the techniques used there – anonymous accounts, detailed operational instructions, automated amplification and the rapid disappearance of the original network – bear an obvious resemblance to methods repeatedly used by Israeli firms and state-backed operations elsewhere.
The question is not whether Israel possesses the machinery to manipulate foreign politics in this way. It unquestionably does.
The question is whether that machinery was deployed here.
Subscribe now

## A plan to help Morocco “reclaim its north”
There is another striking piece of context.
In April 2026, the Israeli news outlet Ynet published an article headlined: “Abraham Accords reach the Strait: how Israel can help Morocco reclaim its north.”
It was written by a Morocco-based analyst affiliated with the hard-right US-based Middle East Forum, which has previously supported the far-right British figure Tommy Robinson.
The article described developments in Washington as the “architecture of a coordinated strategic repositioning”. It argued that Israel was uniquely placed to help Morocco exploit Spain’s deteriorating relationships with Washington and Jerusalem.
The author proposed three roles for Israel:

- direct diplomatic signalling in support of Morocco’s position;

- lobbying and amplification within Washington;

- repeated attacks on Spain as hypocritical for criticising Israeli territorial policy while retaining Ceuta and Melilla.
He concluded that Israeli support for Morocco’s claim would both impose a political cost on Spain and strengthen a partner with a strategically important position on the Strait of Gibraltar.
Israel has also adopted a strategy of promoting the European far right and its anti-migrant narratives. That includes Vox - the Spanish far-right party which has a militant pro-Israel orientation, and which has links with Netanyahu’s Likud party.
In an interview on Fox News’ Hang Out with Sean Hannity, Netanyahu cited someone who had supposedly been asked:

> “Why are you studying Arabic?”
The answer:

> “Because I want to be able to go to London and Paris.”
Netanyahu continued:

> “If you lose control over your borders, you lose control over your fate and your destiny and your future.”
To be clear, just 0.8 per cent of Londoners use Arabic as their main language, while Arab people make up around 1.6 per cent of the city’s population.
This was Netanyahu scaremongering about a supposed Arab invasion of Europe – the same narrative being used to exploit the Ceuta crisis.
Subscribe now

## Spanish suspicions
Spanish politicians have themselves voiced suspicions about what happened.
After Danny Danon attacked Spain over Ceuta, the Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente responded:

> “Well, things are starting to get pretty clear.”
The implication was obvious: Puente was hinting at Israeli involvement.
Gabriel Rufián, a left-wing Spanish politician, posted:

> “The Moroccan dictatorship, in the service of the US and Israel, is once again blackmailing Spain and Europe this summer by turning its own people into disposable cannon fodder.
“Something that, instead of being the subject of partisan politicking, should be the subject of a cross-cutting State pact.”
Spanish experts have raised similar questions.
Pedro Rodríguez, a professor of international relations, said that the crisis occurred because “Morocco wanted it to happen”. He described it as a display of strategic realignment in which Morocco was aligning itself with the United States and Israel while demonstrating Spain’s inability to control its own territory.
And Kenneth Roth - former executive director of Human Rights Watch - posted:

> “Why would Israel want its ally Morocco to control Ceuta as opposed to its critic Spain? One reason may be that Ceuta is the closest point in Africa to Europe, sitting astride the Strait of Gibraltar, meaning that Spain currently controls both sides of the strait. The Strait of Gibraltar is only 8 miles across, as opposed to the Strait of Hormuz, which is 21 miles. If Iran can control the Strait of Hormuz, Spain could easily control the Strait of Gibraltar and potentially block Israeli access to the Atlantic.”
Subscribe now

## What can we conclude?
None of this proves for certain that Israel or the US helped orchestrate the crisis. That caveat matters.
But it would be equally unserious to dismiss the possibility out of hand.
Morocco is a close US and Israeli ally, with deep security and intelligence ties to both states. It has previously facilitated mass crossings into Ceuta to extract political concessions from Spain. On this occasion, its security forces were visibly passive until tens of thousands of people had crossed – and then demonstrated that they were entirely capable of stopping the movement.
Washington had just increased military and economic support for Morocco, financed a project in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara and endorsed language treating Ceuta and Melilla as territories whose future status should be negotiated.
Senior US and Israeli figures immediately seized on the crisis to attack Spain and promote the idea of an Arab “invasion” of Europe.
Anonymous social-media accounts of unknown origin played a crucial role in mobilising people, providing practical instructions and spreading the claim that the border was open. Many of those accounts then vanished. Israel has an extensive record of state-backed and private influence operations using precisely these methods.
That does not prove the case.
At the very least, Israel, the US and the far-right in general have shamelessly exploited this crisis.
Whether that involvement goes deeper surely demands investigation.

reads.title: No, Trump Did Not Explode at His Advisers Inside the Situation Room. That “Leak” Is Engineered, and the Tradecraft Gives It Away.
reads.subtitle: A verbatim account of what a president said inside a SCIF during a war does not slip out by accident. It slips out on purpose, and the question is never whether it is true. It is who benefits...
reads.body:
A story is circulating that the president exploded at his advisers inside a national security meeting, screaming, cornered, out of options. It has everything a viral leak needs: drama, a tidy narrative arc, the frisson of the forbidden glimpse. It is also, on the evidence of how it is structured and how it is travelling, almost certainly not what it presents itself as.
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Let me explain how the tradecraft gives it away, and then why someone wanted you to believe it. Because the mechanics of this story matter more than its content, and reading the mechanics is the difference between being an audience for an operation and being an analyst of one.

-
-
> Where these meetings actually happen
Start with the room, because the room is the first tell. National security deliberations of this kind take place inside a SCIF, a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility. The White House Situation Room is one such SCIF. These are not ordinary rooms with a sensitive conversation happening in them. They are purpose-built containment environments.
No personal phones. No recording devices. Walls shielded to defeat electronic emanation, a discipline the intelligence community calls TEMPEST, so that not even the electromagnetic ghost of a conversation escapes. Access is restricted to a small number of cleared individuals, admitted on strict need-to-know, holding clearances at the top-secret level and above.
Get 7 day free trial
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Now think about what a verbatim leak from that environment would actually represent. Not a staffer’s vague impression relayed over drinks. A clean, quotable account of what the president said, inside a SCIF, during an active war. That does not slip out by accident, because the architecture of the room exists precisely to make accidental escape impossible.

> Why a real breach would look nothing like this
Here is the reasoning that turns suspicion into assessment. If a genuine verbatim account of a wartime SCIF deliberation had escaped, it would be one of the gravest security breaches in modern White House history, and the response would be immediate and overwhelming. A counterintelligence investigation would open within hours.
The FBI and the intelligence community would treat it as a potential espionage matter, not a public-relations embarrassment. Everyone with access to that room would face polygraphs almost immediately. The universe of suspects is tiny by design, which makes a leaker far easier to catch than in an ordinary office, not harder. And the penalty is not reputational. Disclosing national defense information of this kind sits in the territory of the Espionage Act: loss of clearance, loss of career, loss of pension, and years in federal prison.
Everyone with access to that room knows all of this in their bones. So hold the two facts side by side. The room is sealed to the point of paranoia, and the penalty for breaching it is career-ending prison. And yet this account is circulating freely, cleanly, with a dramatic story neatly attached, and no manhunt is visibly under way, no clearances visibly suspended, no counterintelligence spasm in evidence.
Leave a comment
Share
That combination is the anomaly. A real breach of this magnitude is loud on the response side. This one is silent on the response side. Which means one of two things, and both point the same direction. Either it did not come from inside that room at all, or it came out with authorization. A leak that would normally trigger a five-alarm counterintelligence fire, and does not, was not an unauthorized leak.
So ask the question the story is designed to stop you asking
If the penalty is that severe and the room is that sealed, why is this account moving so freely, so cleanly, with such a serviceable dramatic shape, and why has no one been arrested? The narrative discourages you from asking, because it arrives pre-loaded with its own explanation, a president losing control, which is emotionally satisfying enough that most readers stop there. Stopping there is the point. An operation works by giving you a conclusion vivid enough that you never examine the delivery mechanism.
Subscribe now
Because it was very likely never a leak. It was a message, engineered to wear the costume of a leak, and the costume is doing exactly what it was tailored to do.

> What it is actually for: the information-warfare read
This is what I classify, from a strategic realism and intelligence-tradecraft perspective, as information warfare, and once you look at it as an operation rather than as news, its targets become legible. It is aimed in two directions at once, and each vector does distinct work.

- The primary target is Tehran. A story that the American president is losing his temper, cornered, rattled, out of options, performs a specific function against an adversary. It is a deception operation in the classic mold, and the mold is very old. In the tradecraft, this is the deliberate cultivation of a false picture of your own condition, what deception doctrine calls presenting the enemy a flattering read of your disarray.

You feed your opponent an image of yourself as weaker and more chaotic than you are, in the hope that he acts on the image rather than on reality. An overconfident adversary overplays. He pushes when he should hold, escalates when he should wait, commits when he should hedge, because he believes the other side is cracking. Every mistake he makes on the basis of the flattering picture is a mistake he would never have made had he seen you clearly.

Sun Tzu wrote the principle down two and a half thousand years ago: appear weak when you are strong. Nothing about it has changed except the delivery channel, which is now your feed.
Get 7 day free trial
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

- The secondary target is the domestic audience, and this vector is subtler. A lurid palace-intrigue story about a shouting match performs three jobs at home simultaneously. It shapes the public mood, seeding an impression of an administration in turmoil that can be exploited or corrected later as needed. It muddies the water around what is actually being decided, so that the real deliberation, the one that genuinely happened, is obscured by the theatrical one that did not. And it functions as chaff, in the counter-radar sense, flooding the information space with a bright, distracting signal so that the actual signal, the real policy move, passes underneath unwatched while everyone argues about the soap opera. Misdirection is not a bug in this story. It is the entire mechanism.
