In another case, in the Al-Faraa refugee camp in Tubas, the Israeli army shot a 14-year-old Palestinian boy, and when his mother rushed to his help, they shot at her, and then they put a red laser on the head of the paramedics who tried to save his life. He bled to death in front of his mother, surrounded by Israeli soldiers who did nothing to help him and showed no concern about a boy they had shot bleeding to death in front of them.
In Khan Younis, a 15-year-old boy stepped out of his family home holding a white cloth during evacuation. He was shot in the foot, then shot again in the back and neck. His 20-year-old brother ran to him and was shot dead too. His mother tried to signal for an ambulance and was shot in the hand. The Commission says the 15-year-old was likely shot by a sniper rifle from around 200 metres away, and that the shooter should have been able to see he was a child holding a white flag.
Share
A four-year-old girl in Khan Younis was shot in the head while eating with her family in their tent. No one else in the family was injured. She survived but the left side of her body was paralysed. The Commission concluded she was targeted by a quadcopter mounted with an assault rifle.

## Not tragic mistakes - targeted killings
In Sheikh Radwan, the report says Israeli soldiers threw four grenades into a house with 30 family members, badly injuring a five-year-old boy. Israeli forces then entered, shot dead eight family members including his parents, and did not provide medical assistance. A doctor at a school reinserted the child’s exposed intestines using diapers and tape. He later needed multiple surgeries and was left with permanent disability. His six-year-old brother also survived; both had witnessed their parents’ killing, including their pregnant mother being shot.
The report describes the decomposing bodies of four babies found in Al-Nasr Paediatric Hospital’s neonatal intensive care unit after staff were forced to evacuate and could not safely move the most vulnerable infants. The babies were reportedly still attached to life-support equipment rendered useless by the electricity outage and attacks. The Commission says the video was digitally verified and notes that Israel did not claim Al-Nasr Paediatric Hospital was used by Hamas.
After the October 2025 so-called ceasefire, two brothers aged 10 and nine were killed by an Israeli drone strike near Khan Younis while gathering firewood for their wheelchair-bound father. Israeli forces said they were “suspects” and an “immediate threat”. The Commission rejected this, noting they were more than 300 metres from Israeli soldiers, were visibly children, and were collecting firewood.
Note that none of these children are named. Chris Sidoti, an Australian human rights lawyer and one of the UN Commissioners, explained why.
In other words, the UN fears that if they name the children, their families are risk of reprisals from the Israeli army.
Subscribe now

## Killing in the West Bank
This reports builds on the overwhelming evidence of Palestinian children being deliberately targeted and killed by the Israeli army.
In 2024, the NGO Defence for Children International published a report documenting 141 Palestinian children killed by Israeli forces and settlers in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, between 7 October 2023 and 31 July 2024.
116 of the 141 children were shot dead with live ammunition or by snipers. DCIP says nearly all were shot in the head or torso, and 18 were shot in the back, which it describes as “a crystal clear indicator” that the child posed no threat.
Most were killed with a single bullet either to the head or the torso., which DCIP says indicates shooters targeted them “with intent to kill.” They described how Israeli forces “order Palestinian paramedics and ambulance drivers to leave the scene at gunpoint”, as well as firing at people trying to offer aid to injured children, as well as blocking roads and detaining ambulance crews.
In some of the cases, Israeli soldiers surrounded children they had shot as they bled out, “alone and in pain, with the intent to ensure death”.
Subscribe now
It says there is no evidence warnings were issued by Israeli forces in advance, and that the evidence “indicates that Israeli forces in practice have a policy in place that amounts to wilful killing.”
A report just published by Israeli human rights’ organisation B’Tselem finds that 235 Palestinian children and teenagers were killed in the West Bank since October 2023, with another 5 killed by settlers.
In nearly a quarter of the cases they examined, Israel delayed or completely prevented medics or residents from reached wounded children to offer help.
Nine minors, including two girls, were killed during military raids where no arrests were made.

## What the doctors saw
There are the testimonies of doctors. A New York Times piece in October 2024 carried the testimonies of dozens of US-based medical staff who served in Gaza. 44 of them testified that they saw “multiple cases of preteen children who had been shot in the head or chest in Gaza”.”
, too. I interviewed Dr. Nick Maynard, for example, a leading consultant surgeon from Oxford who served in Gaza three times during the genocide.
Subscribe now
He described treating “very young teenage boys, sometimes as young as 11 or 12,” shot by Israeli soldiers and quadcopters while trying to get food for their starving families at Gaza Humanitarian Foundation sites. What horrified him most was the pattern: one day boys arrived with gunshot wounds “to the head,” another “to the neck,” another “to the chest or the abdomen,” and on one day four young teenage boys arrived together with gunshot wounds “to the testicles.” The “clustering” was so striking, he said, that it was “inconceivable that it was coincidence”: it looked like “some sort of obscene target practice,” with Israeli soldiers “playing a game.” Maynard added: “I would not have thought it possible if I had not seen this with my own eyes.”
Meanwhile, Jewish-American surgeon Mark Perlmutter - who also served in Gaza - testified that Israeli snipers are deliberately targeting children in Gaza. Recalling witnessing children shot twice, he said: “No child gets shot twice by mistake.”
And even despite the BBC’s dire failures, the World Service year examined 160 cases of children being shot in Gaza. They found that in 95 cases, the child was shot int he head or the chest, and in most cases, they were under 12 years old.

## The society that justifies killing children
We could go on. The evidence is overwhelming and incontrovertible.
We are told that it is a “blood libel” to state this obvious fact.
So consider this. According to a poll last year, 76% of Jewish Israelis believe there are no innocents in Gaza.
Process that again: no innocents in Gaza. That, of course, includes children and babies.
In another poll, 47% of Jewish Israelis answered yes to the question:

> Do you support the claim that the [Israeli army] in conquering an enemy city, should act in a manner similar to the way the Israelites did when they conquered Jericho under the leadership of Joshua, ie to kill all its inhabitants?
In other words, half of Jewish Israelis support killing all Palestinians in Gaza. That includes those, of course, who are actually serving in the military.
But what makes this even worse is that polling consistently shows that Israeli soldiers are more extreme than the average Israeli citizens.
The polling shows that soldiers skew right. That is partly because - unlike in many societies - younger Israelis tend to be more extreme than older generations.
Subscribe now

## Every child becomes the enemy
Furthermore, Israeli television frequently features guests who make clear their murderous intentions towards children, partly on the basis they claim they will one day become “terrorists”. (This is exactly the same logic the Nazis used during the Holocaust).
In one interview, the Israeli politician Amit Halevi - a member of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, said:

> In the Al-Shifa Hospital, they caught 150 terrorists and killed them. At the same time, 300 terrorists were born in the maternity ward.
On Israel’s Channel 14, while commenting on footage of devastation in Gaza, Israeli journalist Yaki Adamker said:

> I do not think anyone in the State of Israel, in the Land of Israel should feel sorry for these Gazans, not for the adults, not for the elderly, not for the young, and not for the children (...) The Gazans? For all I care, let them starve to death. What do I care about them?
Another Channel 14 journalist, Yehuda Schlesinger said:

> There are no innocents in Gaza. There are no ordinary citizens in Gaza. Every adult was trained to kill. Every woman is a monster. Every boy aspires to be a martyr Every baby will grow up to be a terrorist. wipe out, kill, destroy, annihilate.
In another example, Israeli politician Moshe Feiglin went on Channel 14 to say: “Every child in Gaza is the enemy.” He added: “Every child you are now giving milk to will, in 15 years, rape your daughters and slaughter your children,” as well as calling to conquer and settle Gaza so “not one Gazan child remains there”.
This is the genocidal hothouse of Israeli society - where politicians and journalists openly describe their murderous intent towards children.
There is no doubt. Israel is deliberately killing Palestinian children on a mass scale - and the atrocity deniers who claim otherwise must be disgraced.

reads.title: Trump Is Asking the Gulf for $300 Billion to 'Make Iran Great Again'. The Gulf Will Not Bite. Here Is Why the MOU Cannot Materialise.
reads.subtitle: Everyone is asking what the $300 billion will buy. Nobody is asking why the $300 billion cannot structurally materialise. The Gulf states will not finance the rise of their regional adversary.
reads.body:
I wrote previously that America’s only off-ramp from the Iran war runs through Riyadh. The Trump administration appears to have absorbed that analytical reality. During the MOU signing ceremony Pakistan and the United States both thanked Riyadh profusely. The Saudi institutional role in producing the framework was publicly acknowledged for the first time after months of operating through quiet bilateral channels.
But Trump took the architecture one step further than the Saudi off-ramp logic supported.

-
-
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
The administration has reportedly asked the Gulf Cooperation Council member states to cough up $300 billion USD as the financial mechanism for the Iranian war reparations component of the MOU framework. The framework characterises the $300 billion as “investment in Iranian reconstruction” and as the price for opening the Strait of Hormuz to its previous transit state. The structural reality is that the strait was already open on February 27, 2026 before the Iran war began. The framework asks the Gulf states to pay $300 billion for an outcome that the documented record indicates already existed before the conflict.
Everyone in the analytical commentary is asking what the $300 billion will buy. Nobody is asking why the $300 billion cannot structurally materialise. This piece walks the five structural reasons that the Gulf states will not finance the framework, the realist analytical conclusion that the MOU cannot deliver the operational outcome it requires, and the broader structural implication that the Trump administration appears to have miscalculated what the Gulf institutional architecture will actually support.

> The first structural reason. The Gulf states will not finance the rise of their regional adversary.
The Gulf Cooperation Council member states have spent the past 47 years operating within a security architecture that treats Iranian institutional capacity as the primary regional threat. The Saudi, Emirati, Bahraini, Kuwaiti, Qatari, and Omani institutional architectures have each calibrated their foreign policy positioning, their military procurement, their alliance commitments, and their broader strategic frameworks against the structural reality of Iranian regional positioning.
The proposed $300 billion fund asks these institutional architectures to do the opposite of what 47 years of strategic positioning has required. Rather than constraining Iranian institutional capacity, the fund would directly finance Iranian reconstruction and therefore directly fund the rise of the regional adversary the Gulf states have been positioning against.
The realist analytical conclusion is that no Gulf state can sign that financing commitment without producing immediate domestic political crisis, immediate regional alliance fracture, and immediate questions about whether the broader Gulf state strategic positioning across the past 47 years was correct. The institutional consequences of signing the financing commitment exceed any structural benefit the framework could deliver.

> The second structural reason. The Gulf states would rather pay America to finish the job than pay Iran to rebuild.
If the Gulf states were going to mobilise $300 billion for the Iran file, the realist analytical framework predicts they would prefer to direct the resources toward producing the strategic outcomes that 47 years of positioning have sought rather than toward financing the institutional reconstruction of the adversary.
Subscribe now
The Saudi institutional architecture has been signalling across multiple files that it views Iranian institutional change as the optimal strategic outcome. The Emirati institutional architecture has been operating through similar positioning. The Qatari institutional architecture has been more accommodating to Tehran historically but has not signalled willingness to finance Iranian institutional restoration at the scale the framework requires.
The covert preference across the Gulf institutional architecture is to direct resources toward completing the Iranian institutional change that the probing operations of 2025 and 2026 did not deliver rather than toward financing the institutional restoration that would reverse the gains those operations produced. The framework asks the Gulf states to do the opposite of their preferred strategic outcome. Realist analysis predicts the framework will not survive contact with Gulf state institutional decision-making.

> The third structural reason. If the framework materialises, the Gulf states cut out America as the middleman.
The realist analytical framework requires examining what happens if the Gulf states do mobilise the $300 billion despite the structural arguments against doing so. The answer is that they cut out America as the middleman because the broader strategic logic requires it.
If Iran emerges from the framework with substantial restored institutional capacity and the Gulf states have financed that restoration, the Gulf institutional calculation shifts fundamentally. The Gulf states will recognise that the regional power architecture has changed. Iran will operate as the rising regional power. The Gulf states will be Iran’s geographic neighbours with documented cultural exchange since the emergence of Islam. The bilateral Gulf-Iran institutional architecture will displace the trilateral Gulf-America-Iran architecture that the current framework constructs.
The American institutional architecture operates within four-year electoral cycles with two-year midterm constraints. The Iranian institutional architecture operates within multi-generational timeframes. The Gulf institutional architecture calibrates against the longer institutional time horizon when forced to choose. If the framework restores Iranian institutional capacity, the Gulf states pivot to bilateral arrangements with Tehran and progressively reduce their dependence on American institutional intermediation across the regional architecture.
This is the structural outcome the framework actually produces if it succeeds. The Trump administration appears not to have analysed this dimension. The realist analytical conclusion is that even framework success produces strategic American defeat across the regional architecture.

> The fourth structural reason. The Unity of Arenas doctrine cannot be bought.
Iran has spent at least 30+ years building the Unity of Arenas doctrinal architecture that coordinates pressure across Iranian-aligned fronts simultaneously. The doctrine includes Hezbollah operational coordination in Lebanon, Houthi operational coordination in Yemen, Iraqi Popular Mobilisation Forces operational coordination across the broader theatre, Palestinian factions operational coordination, and the broader Axis of Resistance institutional architecture.
The framework asks Iran to dismantle or operationally subordinate this doctrinal architecture in exchange for the $300 billion fund and the broader concession architecture. The Iranian institutional consensus that has held across the Khamenei era and the post-Khamenei transition under Mojtaba Khamenei since March 8, 2026 will not accept dismantling the Unity of Arenas because the doctrine is the institutional foundation of Iranian regional positioning.
The Iranian institutional architecture will accept tactical throttling of proxy activity to maintain framework viability. The Iranian institutional architecture will not accept strategic dismantling of the doctrinal infrastructure that 47 years of investment produced. The framework therefore cannot deliver the operational outcome it requires regardless of whether the $300 billion materialises.

> The fifth structural reason. The Hormuz routing has already been operationally contested.
The framework’s nominal commitment to opening the Strait of Hormuz to previous transit conditions has already been operationally contested across the past 72 hours. The IMO-Oman corridor launched on June 24, 2026 was struck by an Iranian projectile on June 25, 2026 according to US officials. The IMO Secretary General paused the evacuation framework for 11,000 stranded seafarers within hours. The Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held a bilateral call with Omani Foreign Minister Badr Al-Busaidi on June 26 to discuss continuing framework discussions on Strait of Hormuz administration and maritime services.
The structural reality is that Iran controls Hormuz transit through the documented operational capability validated across the 117-day conflict period. Any Hormuz arrangement requires Iranian institutional acceptance regardless of how much money the Gulf states commit to financing alternative arrangements. The framework cannot purchase what Iran controls operationally.

> The realist analytical conclusion
The $300 billion fund cannot and will not materialise because the Gulf states will not finance the rise of their regional adversary, because the Gulf preference is to direct resources toward Iranian institutional change rather than toward Iranian institutional restoration, because framework success would produce structural American displacement from the regional architecture, because the Unity of Arenas doctrine cannot be purchased through external concession, and because the Hormuz routing has already been operationally contested by Iranian institutional action.
The Trump administration appears to have made two analytical errors in constructing the framework. The first error was assuming the Gulf states would finance the Iranian institutional restoration that the framework requires. The second error was assuming the Iranian institutional architecture would accept dismantling the Unity of Arenas in exchange for the financing arrangement.

reads.title: Prediction: Oman Sides With Iran on Hormuz Fees Within 24 Months. The Public Denials Technically Allow It.
reads.subtitle: UNCLOS lets Oman charge for services while denying transit tolls. The June 25 strike and the June 26 call show the bilateral framework is already operationally active. Here is the timeline.
reads.body:
I have been to Oman and have driven across the country on business trips at least once per year in the past 10 years hence I am sharing this analysis with a deeper knowledge of how the society works, thinks and functions. But first, this analysis has to start with the timelines of the past week that I monitored:
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

- On Sunday, Trump declared the Strait of Hormuz “permanently toll-free”.

- On Wednesday, While in Bahrain, Marco Rubio reinforced the position at the Bahrain GCC meeting. Omani Foreign Minister (FM) Badr Al-Busaidi publicly aligned with this narrative at the same meeting.  The joint GCC statement rejected any tolls, fees, or attempts to assert control over the strait.

- On Thursday: Iran fired a projectile at a Singapore-flagged cargo vessel on the new IMO-Oman corridor off Dahit area. The IMO paused its evacuation of 11,000 stranded seafarers within hours.

- On Friday, Iranian FM Abbas Araghchi held what he called a “productive call” with Omani FM Al-Busaidi to define future administration and maritime services in the Strait of Hormuz.
The cameras show the public consensus. The realpolitik underneath shows something different. The framework discussions moved out of the public diplomatic theatre and into the private bilateral channel where actual decisions are made.
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
This piece walks why Oman WILL side with Iran on the Hormuz fee framework over the medium term. The argument anchors in four pillars:

- The historical relationships.

- The trade data trajectories.

- The Oman Vision 2040 economic calculation and consideration.

- The American leverage constraints.
The June 25 strike and the June 26 call confirm the structural prediction operationally. Let me walk you through my thinking.

> Oman never said it would charge a fee (publicly)
The Oman fee story did not come from Muscat. It came from Iranian state media, then got laundered through English-language outlets. Yet Trump said on May 27 that Oman will behave “just like everybody else or we will have to blow them up”. The State Department confirmed he meant Oman by posting the transcript. Treasury Secretary Bessent warned on May 28 that the US would ‘aggressively target anyone facilitating tolls’.
The realist significance is direct. The United States threatened to bomb “the Switzerland” of the Middle East over a position Muscat had NOT publicly taken. Oman hosted the original US-Iran nuclear back channels, mediated between the Houthis and the Saudis, and kept its embassy open in Tehran while maintaining a warm relationship with Washington across decades. Imagine London or Berlin announcing that Geneva would be bombed if the actual Switzerland kept talking to Russia. The architecture of neutral diplomacy would be treated as under attack because it would be.
Subscribe now
The GCC silence reinforced the threat through collective non-defence of a founding member. Sovereignty that is not defended is sovereignty being surrendered in instalments.

> The 400-year neighbour relationship
Oman and Iran have shared the Strait of Hormuz as bilateral neighbours since before the founding of the United States. The realist significance is institutional rather than symbolic. Omani decision-makers operate within a strategic culture that calibrates relationships across multi-generational timeframes. American administrations operate within four-year electoral cycles with two-year midterm constraints. We need to understand this difference in time horizons.
Trust is the regional currency. The Iranian institutional commitment to Oman has been demonstrated across the 1979 revolution, the Iran-Iraq war, the 2015 nuclear deal, the 2018 collapse, and the 2024 to 2026 war. The American institutional commitment has shown substantially greater volatility across administration transitions. Trump’s May 27 bombing threat and Bessent’s sanctions warning operationalised that volatility in ways Muscat cannot ignore.
Realist logic calibrates against the CONSISTENT counterparty over the VOLATILE one. This is NOT anti-American positioning. This is realpolitik applied to bilateral relationship management.

> The trade data tells the story
Iran-Oman bilateral trade reached approximately $1.35 billion in the first 10 months of 2025 per Oman’s National Centre for Statistics and Information, up 24% year-on-year. Iran ranks as the second-largest destination for Omani re-exports after the UAE, with re-exports accounting for 21% of Oman’s total.
Iranian exports to Oman ($394 million in the first seven months of 2025) exceed American exports to Oman ($218 million in the same period).
The US-Oman trade volume runs approximately $5 to $7 billion annually, substantially larger than the direct Iran-Oman volume. But realist analysis weights the trajectory over the level. Iran-Oman is growing 24 percent year-on-year. US-Oman has been flat for five years. The direction of movement determines strategic calculation more than the absolute position does.

-
-
> The June 25 strike changes the operational reality
The IMO-Oman corridor is the operational alternative to the Iran-designated route. By firing on a vessel using it, Iran demonstrated that any alternative is kinetically contested. Any Omani service-based fee architecture must therefore operate within the structural reality that Iran can disrupt arrangements that do not include Iranian institutional acceptance.
Leave a comment
This actually reinforces rather than weakens my realist thesis. Oman cannot operationalise the fee architecture without Iranian cooperation because the geographic and military reality of the Strait makes coordination structurally necessary. The American opposition therefore cannot prevent the framework. It can only delay or modify the implementation timeline.
The FMs Araghchi-Al-Busaidi call confirms the pattern. Iran fired on a vessel using the IMO route on Thursday. Iran called the Omani Foreign Minister on Friday. The bilateral framework is operationally active.

> The economic calculation and Vision 2040
The Hormuz fee architecture could plausibly generate $5 to $20 billion annually for Oman in a high-leverage scenario where service fees apply across the approximately 20 percent of global oil trade transiting the strait. Against Oman’s $108 billion GDP in 2024, this represents 4 to 16 percent of national output.

-
- Oman’s Vision 2040 framework explicitly targets diversification away from oil toward services, logistics, and value-added activities. The fee architecture under bilateral discussion creates exactly the economic activity Vision 2040 frames as strategic priority. Maritime services. Pollution response. Navigation aids. Insurance and risk management. The Oman Investment Authority manages approximately $50 billion. Fee revenue would compound sovereign wealth accumulation across multiple decades.
Subscribe now

This piece walks the historical theology, the captured state architectures, the co-dependent transaction between the two factions, the resource-and-strategy layer underneath, and the structural implication that the exit from this war cannot come from the people inside it.

The position holds that the believer can and should engineer the conditions for the Mahdi’s return. The conditions include the defeat of the United States and Israel. The position is variously labeled apocalyptic Mahdism, accelerationist Mahdism, or simply Mahdism in modern Iranian political discourse.
The Paydari Front, formally known as the Front of Islamic Revolution Stability, is the institutional vehicle for this current within contemporary Iranian politics. The Front emerged in 2011 during the Ahmadinejad-Khamenei tensions. The Front has progressively consolidated institutional position across the Iranian state architecture over the past decade. The Front’s ideology explicitly includes Mahdist accelerationism among its core doctrinal commitments.
Front of Islamic Revolution StabilityMojtaba Khamenei was installed as Supreme Leader on March 8, 2026 under IRGC institutional pressure after the assassination of his father Ali Khamenei. Mojtaba is the documented patron of the Paydari Front. The apocalyptic faction won the Iranian succession. The destruction of Israel for this faction is not a political objective. Commentary .02 of Rule 6.77 also states that once both parties agree to the trade nullification, one party must “promptly notify the Exchange for dissemination of cancellation information to the Options Price Reporting Authority.” In addition, the Exchange currently allows for a mutual price adjustment for trades that meet the obvious error (or catastrophic error) requirements pursuant to Exchange Rule 6.87 if those mutual agreements are done within specific timeframes.”
Unfortunately it is not specified if the trade in question has been outright nullified or if a modification has been made.
In this specific example we see, shortly after the nullification/modification, another trade on the same contract.
We can reason that in this case the trade was modified rather than nullified, given that we are seeing a similarly looking transaction on the tape.
As a reminder: as previously stated nothing explicitly states whether a trade has been outright nullified or if a modification has been made. If some flow you’re tracking receives a red strike out make sure to pour over the flow feed to try and identify a modification. If no modification is visible then it’s likely the trade was nullified.

reads.title: I warned you Starmer would implode in office
reads.subtitle: I don't care if this sounds smug. I predicted what should have been obvious
reads.body:
- Years before he entered No. 10, it was obvious that Keir Starmer’s project would end in catastrophe. It was entirely predictable - and indeed, predicted.
Well, by those of us on the left. Not by the vast majority of “mainstream” commentators.
I told you so’s are always undignified. I offer no apologies. These predictions were ridiculed at the time - but we can’t move forward unless it’s understood why Starmerism has fallen apart.
In years of Opposition, Starmer proved that his project was always defined by dishonesty, that it had no vision for the country, and that its arrogant architects weren’t even up to the job.
BattleLines with Owen Jones is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
A caveat. I didn’t vote for Keir Starmer to become Labour leader - I voted for the left-wing standard-bearer Rebecca Long-Bailey. When he won the 2020 leadership contest, I nonetheless accepted his victory in good faith, conditional on him sticking by his leadership pledges.
The political direction of his leadership swiftly became very clear. Here is what I criticised - and predicted.
In October 2020, after Labour abstained on a Conservative bill making it legal for undercover agents to commit sexual assault, torture and murder, I wrote:

> For the second time in as many weeks, Labour offered a vacuum in place of leadership against state-sanctioned violence against civilians. It has paid a profound moral price, and conceded yet more ground to its opponents.
(I should note that, in this period, Keir Starmer would repeatedly contact me to object to my criticisms, in one case telling me I was better than this).
In February 2021, I wrote a piece headlined ‘By ignoring young voters, Labour is creating an opening for the Greens’.
I warned:

> If the new Labour leadership insists on alienating young people who prefer a strong state to intervene to achieve greater economic and social equality, and transition to a greener economy in order to reduce the impact of the climate crisis, then it may find, as in Scotland and with the red wall, another chunk of Labour’s electoral coalition finds somewhere else to go. A similar phenomenon is happening in Wales, where Plaid Cymru is on the rise and nearly half of young Welsh citizens support independence.
Share
The same month, I wrote that Starmer’s Labour had placed itself to the right of the Tories on tax, adding:

> Labour’s opposition to tax increases is yet another illustration of an increasingly obvious truth: the party’s leadership lacks a political soul and is devoid of any meaningful coherent vision for the country it seeks to lead.
I added:

> Political direction is coming from the focus groups because Starmer’s team lacks a political vision to guide them. They desperately want to win power, but they don’t know why.
And concluded:

> Instead, the Labour leadership seeks power without a vision. That is, to be fair, an interesting political experiment, but one that is unlikely to end well. It is not too late to change course.
In May 2021, I wrote:

> Starmer’s team are on safari, knowing nothing about communities they didn’t grow up in, leading to cosplay, caricature and flag-waving, which screeches inauthenticity and nothing more.
Subscribe now
The same month:

> After a year as leader, Starmer has shown a lack of political vision, a thin-skinned aversion to criticism, and an over-dependence on a small circle of inexperienced advisers, all of which have been on display over the past few days.
Then in June 2021:

> Many Muslims, like many young people, who felt listened to under Corbyn’s leadership now feel sidelined, only deemed of use as voting fodder. Whether in this byelection or next time around, they want to give Labour a kicking until they are listened to. That is, after all, how many diehard Scottish Labour voters felt: but when they crossed the electoral Rubicon, they never came back.
In September 2021, I wrote about Starmer’s dishonesty:

> Dishonesty corrodes democracy like acid. If politicians make promises they renege on, voters conclude that none can be trusted and disengage from the political process. Accountability – a prerequisite of any functioning democracy – becomes impossible, because if dishonesty is normalised, a priced-in background hum of politics, then objections to the stench of deceit can be shrugged off by politicians on the grounds that all of their colleagues are in the sewer, too.
I added:

> When I described Starmer’s team as “maniacs” because of their abortive attempts to reintroduce an electoral college granting MPs disproportionate power in the next leadership election, a shadow minister responded to me: “It’s worse than that: they are incompetent.” Starmer, whose own allies describe him as a man without politics, is surrounded by crude factional figures with an obsessive grudge against the left and no vision for the country.
And I further added:

> There is nothing to recommend Starmer’s leadership. He is, as we have seen, unprincipled. He is not honest. Where Blair and Neil Kinnock were talented orators, Starmer lacks any charisma or warmth. He extolled “integrity” in the leadership election, but as his sacking in May of deputy leader Angela Rayner from her role as Labour chair underlined, he has none. That more Labour voters than not desire his resignation, that more than six in 10 people do not see him as a prime minister in waiting, and that he lost the Hartlepool byelection – a seat Labour retained even in the landslide defeat of 2019 – shows he is unelectable. Starmer is Labour’s version of Theresa May – who was originally lauded as a serious, public-spirited politician before being undone by her own cynicism and woodenness.
Subscribe now
What I got wrong here was about Starmer being unelectable. But this was entirely down to the Tories’ self-destruction. The column was written before partygate and all of the other Boris Johnson scandals which destroyed him. It was written before the Liz Truss catastrophe. And then there was the return of a ferocious squeeze in living standards, and a collapsing NHS - and all the dire failures of the Rishi Sunak era.
And yet despite being handed the election on a platter - and indeed the Tories’ calamitous election campaign - Labour only won a third of the vote on a dire turnout. They were saved by Nigel Farage dividing the right-of-centre vote.
The points I was making here - about Labour’s dishonesty, their lack of vision for the country, their hatred of the left, and Starmer’s own lack of leadership qualities - are exactly why it all fell apart.
In February 2023, I wrote:

>  While Starmer’s team behaves as though it’s 1997, Britain’s current state is more like 1974 – that is, in crisis and turmoil. If a Labour government offers only tinkering around the edges of the economy, and the lives of struggling households do not substantially improve, mass disillusionment may soon kick in. It remains the case that the most interesting ideas are bubbling away on the left: banishing them from Labour’s future is an act of self-harm. If a meek Starmer administration disappoints, a now cowed left may find an audience willing to listen. Starmer’s team is buoyant now, and understandably so: but history tell us where hubris leads.
Again, I noted Labour’s lack of vision for the country - and how the left could win an audience as a consequence. We can now see that with the surge of Zack Polanski’s Green Party.
Here’s what I wrote in October 2023, when Labour had a colossal opinion poll lead:

> So consider this for a scenario. Labour triumphs at the next election, but wins by default and with no enthusiasm for Starmerism in the tank from the start. Unlike 1997, the new administration rules a country defined by turmoil and decline, but offers no transformative policies to answer our multiple and overlapping crises. Disillusionment sets in, while the Tories complete their metamorphosis into loud, proud, brash rightwing populism, hoovering up votes from the disaffected. In the general election of 2029, a new model Tory party – flushed with British Trumpism – stages a stunning comeback.
True, this is not the US: your gut instinct may say it can’t happen here. But when, in the past, you looked in bemused horror at their culture wars, you may have assumed they’d never arrive on our shores – but they did. Farage marched through conference not as a hostile outsider, but as a conquering general. His mission is not yet complete, however, and a final prize may beckon.
What I got wrong here was the suggestion that Nigel Farage could take over the Tories. But my basic point -  a government with no answers to a turmoil-afflicted country would open the door to a Farageist insurgency - was obviously correct.
Subscribe now
Here’s what I wrote in December 2023:

> Those hoping this is all one big pretence and, once safely ensconced in No 10, Starmer will yell “Surprise!” and enact a new shiny progressive dawn are set to be most disappointed. And this is now the most interesting question in British politics. When Starmer wins his decisive victory – which he will – and little changes after two years, what happens next?
Alas, there were no shortage of Starmer supporters predicting he would enact a shiny new progressive dawn. Here’s Andrew Marr predicted Starmer would be a “radical” prime minister - two months after I penned that column. Alas, it was not to be!
A day after Andrew Marr’s video, in February 2024, I wrote the following:

> An administration that lacks meaningful answers to domestic crises and is wedded to a toxic foreign policy will soon find itself in trouble. Look at Starmer’s political equivalents in the US, Germany and Australia: they won but swiftly became unpopular, and none U-turned so comprehensively as him on their original promises. If he enjoys a honeymoon, it will be short-lived.
And here was a key point - Starmer-like politics in Germany was particularly instructive, given the insurgency of the far-right AfD. But of course we also saw what happened to Joe Biden.
Just after the general election was called, I wrote:

> Labour will win this election not because there is any real enthusiasm for the party’s agenda nor any real belief in Starmer’s capabilities as a leader. It will win because the Tories have set one of the lowest bars in British political history. And then, when Labour is in power, enjoying so little support and enthusiasm among its natural voters, what next? Winning because people wanted to rid themselves of the incumbent party is not the same as winning because you offered a vision that voters rallied behind.
After this week, the mask is off. Labour’s leaders are sending a clear signal that once they have secured No 10, they will behave with the same power-drunk arrogance and the same disregard for democratic norms that they are showing now towards their own MPs. Starmer should consider, for a moment, the cautionary tale of Boris Johnson – another leader who purged his parliamentary party. Yes, he scooped an 80-seat majority. But then, in less than three years, he was driven from office in disgrace, and the Tory party was left in tatters.
Bear in mind, Labour had a 20 point lead in the polls at the time.
But this is indeed what has happened!
Subscribe now
When the election results came in, I noted there was hope:

> Despite the excessive media focus on the Farageist insurgency, the left revolt is just as significant. If the Labour leadership was rational, it would acknowledge this disaffection and seek to reverse the rot. The party, after all, has secured the same share of the vote as in 2019, winning its landslide thanks to Nigel Farage dividing the right and the vagaries of our electoral system. The juxtaposition between its dominance of the House of Commons and the lack of enthusiasm it enjoys in the country will be increasingly felt.
But here’s a prediction. Those surrounding Starmer are too politically defined by their hostility to the left to learn from this. There will be precious little conciliation: quite the reverse. In the coming years, growing numbers of voters will be driven to the Greens and other leftwing formations. As long as leftwing forces in Britain build on this moment and find common cause – yes, a big but – then this could be a new beginning indeed.
As I predicted, Starmer’s team ignored the evidence of disillusionment from the left - and simply doubled down on further antagonising the left.
My view was that the big challenge facing the left was a question of leadership. After Zack Polanski assumed the leadership of the Greens, he did indeed build on this moment.
It should have been obvious that Starmerism was an empty project - a vacuum filled by dishonesty, arrogance and a craving for power for its own sake.
But instead Starmer was treated as a competent, serious “grown-up in the room” who would offer a new found stability. The idea, basically, was that we were trapped in a Tory psychodrama - and when the party was ejected from office, all of that would go away.
The basic problem is that most political journalism treats politics as a soap opera.
It’s driven by personality - who’s up and who’s down - rather than ideas and the realities affecting ordinary citizens. There was no understanding of the crises afflicting this country - and Labour’s lack of answers to them.
That’s why Starmerism was so badly misreported.
The raging dishonesty of Starmerism always told us that this would end in catastrophe.
But political journalists ignored his dishonesty.
Why?
Because he used it to destroy the left - and they admired that, and saw it as smart politics.
None of this is evidence of my prophetic skills. It should have been obvious what would happen. It is a damning failure of political journalism that this was not understood.
(This is an updated version of this piece from last year)

reads.body:
- Forget the World Cup. This is where the real entertainment is right now.
Israel is in meltdown, and so are its cheerleaders. That’s after Donald Trump capitulated to end the illegal Israeli-American war in Iran, agreeing — according to reports — to proposals including permanently ending the war, ending the naval blockade, a $300bn reconstruction plan for Iran, ending sanctions, and allowing the free export of Iranian oil.
This was a war launched to overthrow Iran’s rulers and secure what Trump described as UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER.

-
- Instead, it has ended with Trump signing up to terms which have left the people who spent years inciting this catastrophe - and then cheering on their fantasy as it opened with the mass slaughter of Iranian schoolgirls - in a state of total despair, anguish and terror.
BattleLines with Owen Jones is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
It is not tasteless to find this funny. These people are furious at peace breaking out - after they bet the house on a cataclysmic war which has produced the literal opposite of everything they hoped for.
The unfunny bit is the death and destruction they helped cause.
Let’s start with the United States, shall we?

## Nikki Haley
What about Nikki Haley, Trump’s former US Ambassador to the UN? When the war began, she was beyond delighted. This was a “history-defining” and “legacy-defining” thing that “needed to happen”, she said.
Well, she was certainly right about one thing. This is a legacy-defining and history-defining moment.
With the war she cheered on now over, Haley responded to reports that the deal allows Iran to immediately sell oil by tweeting:

-

## John Podhoretz
Podhoretz has long been a passionate supporter of war with Iran. When Trump first attacked Iran in June 2025, Podhoretz was so delighted that he wrote an article declaring its impact potentially “enormous” and “world historic”, before concluding:

> Trump has said since the assassination attempt in Butler, Pa., that he believes God spared him for a reason.
And now, so do I.
This was—is—the reason.”
John Podhoretz believed that God literally saved Donald Trump from being assassinated so he could bomb Iran.
Parking, for a second, the theological question of why God did not just stop the assassination attempt from happening in the first place: does that mean God spared Trump in order to go to full-blown war with Iran, only for Iran to emerge victorious?
Because Podhoretz is very clear that this is the outcome of the Iran war.
In a video call, another panellist suggested Iran wants “to humiliate Donald Trump and move on to the next president.”
Podhoretz spluttered: “And they’ve already succeeded!”
His conclusion was bitter: “There is no person on Earth who is going to say that America didn’t lose this war” - unless he said, “you are literally a paid agent of MAGA related to Donald Trump or some lunatic who is really excited by the possibility of Trump turning on Israel.
Subscribe now

## John Bolton
What about John Bolton, professional warmonger, George W. Bush’s Ambassador to the UN and Trump’s former National Security Advisor?
Boy, has this man been a supporter of bombing Iran. It is his one true passion in life. “To Stop Iran’s Bomb, Bomb Iran” was the headline of his New York Times column in March 2015.

-
- Just after Trump started the war, he told PBS:
“I’m sorry it took so long finally for somebody to take action. I think the world would have been a much safer place if somebody did it 20 years ago.”
What’s he saying now? He says of Iran:
“They’ve played him like a violin. That’s why they’ve got the deal that they want.”

At the beginning of the war, Trump rang Laura Loomer, a far-right fanatical anti-Muslim bigot named Laura Loomer, who recalled the conversation at the time:

What about Israel?
When the war began, an astonishing 93% of Jewish Israelis supported the war with Iran, with just 3% somewhat opposing it and 1% strongly opposing it.

The Israeli journalist Emily Schrader was ecstatic when the Iran war was launched. She said it was pure elation the part of Israelis, that  “it’s been absolutely incredible” and praised Trump to the hilt.

reads.title: Someone Front Ran Biopharma News for 1,762.96% Gain!
reads.subtitle: News Frontrunner Makes $1 million
reads.body:
Nicholas from the Unusual Whales team, here!
In this issue, we’re going to walk through some very… “well-timed” options flow in uniQure, $QURE, that started hitting the tape days before the FDA news sent the stock absolutely flying.
As many of you may have seen by now, $QURE finished June 17th up 78.44% after the FDA moved AMT-130, uniQure’s gene therapy candidate for Huntington’s disease, back toward a near-term accelerated approval filing path.
For anyone who doesn’t follow biotech and biopharma too closely, this was a pretty major update. AMT-130 has been one of the more closely watched Huntington’s programs, but the regulatory path had become a little bit of a mess after prior FDA feedback made it look like the company may have to go run another trial before getting anywhere close to a filing.
That would have meant more time, more money, and more uncertainty.
Instead, the FDA came back and said uniQure could use its existing 3-year Phase I/II data to support a BLA submission for accelerated approval. In normal people words, the path forward suddenly looked a lot less cooked than it did before, and for a biotech stock that had been trading under that cloud, the market reacted exactly how you’d expect.

-
- But once again, what caught our eye wasn’t just the move after the news. It was the flow before it.
Back on June 5th, we saw 100 contracts of the June 18 2026 $45 call transact at the bid. On its own, that’s not exactly some world-ending order, but 100% of that volume turned into open interest on June 8th.
Then, on June 8th, we saw another 402 contracts trade at the bid, and once again, 100% of that volume carried over into open interest on June 9th, when another 525 contracts transacted and held into the following trading session yet again.
A lot of options volume is just noise. Some of it opens and closes the same day, some of it gets flipped around, some of it looks interesting for 14 seconds and then turns into a big fat helping of nothingburger for dinner.
Looking at net premium, $QURE had mostly been a quieter name, though we did see some pretty major spikes in net call premium over the last month.

-
- Then came June 15th, and the flow got a lot more interesting when another 1,103 contracts transacted, but this batch hit at the ask. This may have led to the assumption that the former flow, predominantly bid-fills, had been shorted (sold to open) and this volume was a closure. Only thing is, all but 3 contracts carried over into open interest on June 16th, and given the consistent position building from before, I wouldn’t be hard-pressed to assume this was all the same trader, and those prior days were longs rather than shorts.

-
- Across all the days combined, the rough average cost of these contracts came out to around $0.27. After the FDA headline, those contracts hit an intraday high of $5.03.
Using the rough premium tied to this flow, around $59,390, this trade turned into more than $1.07 million in profit on their 1,762.96% gain.
Not gonna lie; that is insane.
Now, as always, we can’t say with certainty this was all the same trader. These orders came in across different sessions, and the early trades hit at the bid while the June 15th batch came through at the ask. So, no, I ain’t gonna to pretend we can know something the tape doesn’t tell us; no one actually knows except the trader(s) themselves.
But with most of the volume carrying over on June 5th, another 100% carrying over from June 9th, and the entire June 15th batch carrying over right before the news, it sure looks like someone was building up a position for something.
It’s worth noting that from here, tracking the original flow gets a lot harder. $QURE saw a ton of volume after the news hit, and once the whole chain starts lighting up, it becomes much more difficult to separate the original pre-news positioning from everyone else piling in after the fact. Over 8,800 contracts transacted on June 17th, with only 2,633 carrying over into open interest; there’s a fairly decent chance that this trader took profit with expiration hitting quite literally today.

-
- Whether $QURE holds this move is a separate question entirely. This is still biotech; accelerated approval is not full approval, and AMT-130 still has a regulatory path to work through. These names can rip violently and give back gains just as quickly when expectations shift.
But for this “trader” who stacked up before the FDA news hit, the hard part was already over.
Hey man, maybe it was luck.
As always, I hope you enjoyed this flow review! We actually discussed this very trade on the Unusual Whales trading show, WhaleWatch!
Here is the YouTube version of that episode, and you can also check out all past episodes of our live trading show, WhaleWatch (airing every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at 9am ET on X, YouTube, and Substack) on the Unusual Whales YouTube!

reads.subtitle: He understands media, attention, and the human mind the way an electrical engineer understands a circuit. He is not fighting the truth. He is engineering the environment the truth has to survive in.
reads.body:
- Almost everything written on this question answers the wrong one. People keep asking how a man lies and survives. The better question, the one the intelligence world would ask, is what system he is operating, and why is it performing exactly as designed.
Set aside whether you like the man. That is a different essay. This one is about the craft. And the craft is real, it is old, it is teachable, and it is being run at a level of fluency that deserves to be understood rather than merely condemned.
So let me answer the title directly, then show the work. He gets away with it because he understands media, attention, and the human mind the way an electrical engineer understands a circuit. He is not fighting the truth. He is engineering the environment the truth has to survive in. Read that again!

> Related Articles that you may enjoy!

The engineer’s mind
An electrical engineer does not believe in electricity. He does not need faith. He knows load, resistance, capacity, and the exact point at which a circuit trips, and he builds to those tolerances. He also knows the person flipping the switch, you and I, understands none of it.
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Read the communications operation through that lens and the chaos resolves into design.
The media is NOT treated as a moral arena where “truth wins”. It is treated as a system with measurable tolerances. A known load limit. A predictable failure point under volume. The operator is not asking whether they will believe him. He is asking how much the system can carry BEFORE it can no longer process anything at all!
That is the whole shift. The truth is not the opponent. Your attention is the opponent. And attention is finite, measurable, and exhaustible, which means it CAN be engineered against. The rest of this piece lives inside that one sentence.
The intelligence thought process behind it
This way of thinking did not come from politics. It comes from a much older world, and people who run “information operations” for a living recognise it on sight and I am here to share this knowledge with you.
In the trade there is a discipline called denial and deception.

- Denial is the old instinct. Hide the truth, classify it, lock it away.

- Deception is the more advanced art, and it hides nothing. It shapes what the target perceives is true by managing the volume and the tempo of what reaches him.
Russian doctrine had a word for the mature version.

> Maskirovka.
People translate it as “camouflage”, which undersells it. The real meaning is closer to managing the entire perception of a situation, so the adversary commits his forces against a picture you built for him rather than the ground that is actually there.
The thought process is NOT how do I make them believe my lie. It is how do I make my read of reality the one they act on. Those are different problems, and ONLY the second wins consistently in politics, military and many other trades.
Human intelligence runs the same instinct at the scale of a single person. A skilled investigator does not interrogate by force. He shapes the room, the tempo, the trust, the fatigue, until the source’s own judgment of what is safe to say quietly shifts. The skilled investigator or HUMINT operator manages the source’s perceived reality. The unskilled one asks questions and gets lied to.
Give a gift subscription
Now scale that instinct from one source in one room to a national audience at the speed of a phone. That is what you are watching. Not a man losing control of the facts. A man controlling the information environment the facts arrive into.
Why the brain cooperates
Here is what makes the craft so effective, and it has nothing to do with politics and everything to do with how the mind is built. The operator is not fighting human psychology. He is using it.

- The illusory truth effect. The brain rates a familiar claim as more likely to be true, regardless of whether it is, simply because it has heard it before. Repetition is not persuasion. It is a shortcut the mind takes to save energy, and it can be loaded on purpose.

- The cognitive miser. People do not reason through every claim. The brain is built to conserve effort and reaches for the easiest available answer. Flood the environment and you are not changing minds, you are raising the cost of thinking until the mind takes the cheapest exit it can find.

- Primacy. The first frame of an event becomes the channel everything else flows through. Whoever defines the situation first does not just join the conversation, he builds the room it happens in. Correct the record later and you are still decorating his room.

- The availability heuristic. People judge what is true by what comes to mind fastest, not by what is most accurate. Volume controls what comes to mind fastest. So volume, not accuracy, sets the perceived reality most people carry around.

- Source amnesia. Within days the mind forgets where it heard a thing and keeps the thing. The claim outlives the correction, because the correction was attached to a source the brain already discarded.
Five features of normal, healthy cognition. None of them are flaws you can shame people out of. They are how the instrument is wired. The operator who knows the wiring does not argue with the instrument. He plays it.

> Another article you may enjoy…
The censorship that adds instead of subtracts
Put the intelligence craft and the psychology together and you reach the single most important idea in the field and it has a name. It is called “censorship through noise”.
The old censor removed information. He hid the document, jailed the journalist, cut the broadcast. That model assumed information was scarce, so control meant subtraction.
Share AJ Jaff. Signal, Not Noise!
The modern environment is the reverse. Information is infinite and free. So you do NOT control it by subtracting. You control it by adding. You bury the signal under so much noise that finding the truth costs more than the average mind is willing to pay, and the seeker quietly gives up. Nothing was hidden. Everything was drowned.
That is why the fact-checkers kept losing and most of these websites are now bankrupt. They built a stronger and stronger hammer for a problem that was never a nail. You cannot subtract your way out of a flood.
And the asymmetry is baked in. Then there is Brandolini’s law. Producing a claim costs almost nothing. Refuting it costs an order of magnitude more. So whoever floods holds the energy advantage over everyone correcting him. The corrector runs out of road first. He always does. And the interesting thing about these ideas and theories is that once you learn them, you cannot unlearn them or forget them, but rather it creates a rabbit hole in your mind to learn more about it, because you know how effective it has been against you!
The inversion most people never brace for
Here is the move that decides everything, and it is the line between old propaganda and the modern kind.

reads.title: Hegseth Says No Munitions Shortage. Trump Just Signed a National Defense Threat Determination. Read the Contradiction.
reads.subtitle: Defense Production Act Section 708. ±50% of four critical munitions inventories expended per CSIS. Israel not party to MOU. The reload moves while the peace narrative absorbs the headlines.
reads.body:
Get 7 day free trial
On June 11, 2026, Trump signed Presidential Determination No. 2026-15 invoking the Defense Production Act. The same day Iranian officials and Qatari mediators narrowed key gaps on the Memorandum of Understanding in Tehran. The same day the operational architecture of the 14-point MOU came together.

-
- Memo For the Secretary of War126KB ∙ PDF fileDownloadPresidential Determination and Delegation of
Authority Under Section 708 of the Defense
Production Act of 1950, as AmendedDownloadThe presidential determination was held until June 16 for public release. The MOU was signed in Pakistan digitally on June 14. Vice President Vance worked every American morning network through June 15 and 16 selling the deal. The Geneva signing ceremony is scheduled for Friday June 19.
The reload and the peace narrative are moving in the same week. Read carefully.

> Restack this…
When I track structural indicators across my proprietary 49-indicator framework, the pairing of a peace document with a national defense threat determination in the same week is NOT a contradiction. It is a signature.
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Specifically, it is the signature of “armed peace”, which is one of the escalation ladder configurations I have documented across this library for the past six months.
This is the indicator I have labeled in prior assessments as “settle on paper, reload underneath the table.”
It is one of the configurations that produces high-confidence forecasts of continued kinetic exchange rather than structural peace.
This piece walks the verified facts and connects them to that framework reading.
What the determination actually does
The determination cites “limited production capacity, fragile supply chains, long-lead dependencies, and related production bottlenecks” in the munitions industrial base. It delegates authority to War Secretary Pete Hegseth under Section 708 of the Defense Production Act.
Section 708 is the narrowest tool in the Defence Production Act toolbox. It does not compel companies to produce anything yet. It does not direct allocation of materials. It does not provide capital. What it does is grant an antitrust waiver.
Companies that would otherwise be prohibited under Sherman Act provisions from coordinating production planning can now sit in the same room with the Pentagon, allocate orders among themselves, share supply chain data, and coordinate output schedules without antitrust exposure.
The administration reached for the legal instrument that enables coordination, not the legal instrument that commands production. That choice is the structural data point.

- If you genuinely believed you were exiting the war, you would not need Section 708.

- If you genuinely believed you were entering an emergency surge requiring maximum compulsion, you would have invoked Title I priorities and allocations and Title III capital.
The administration reached for the middle tool. Coordination without compulsion. Mobilization posture without mobilization order not to create panic in the market but to send a strong message to Iran, and perhaps it may also be preparing for a title I invoking or perhaps, it has already done it in Secret with a gag order. This is within the realm of possibility.
The structural contradiction Hegseth could not paper over
Hegseth spent the prior weeks publicly minimizing the munitions shortage. On Face the Nation, the shortage was “a manufactured story that the media wants to peddle.” Stockpiles “are great, and they’re only getting stronger.” Last month he called the munitions issue “foolishly and unhelpfully overstated.”
In April, the same Hegseth testified before the Senate Armed Services Committee that replenishment could take “months to years” depending on the weapon system. The Center for Strategic and International Studies analysis estimates the United States may have expended more than 50% of its inventory of four critical munitions during the 105-day Iran campaign, including Tomahawk missiles. Senator John Cornyn confirmed Tuesday that the Pentagon is “running short of funding they need in order to acquire the weapons.”

-
- Source: https://www.csis.org/analysis/last-rounds-status-key-munitions-iran-war-ceasefire
-
- The presidential determination is the legal opposite of Hegseth’s public denial. The document formalizes a “direct threat to the national defense” finding. That language is statutory. It is not rhetorical. The institutional planners who know the real burn rate won the argument over the public messaging.
Why June 11 matters specifically
The June 11 signature date is the same day Iranian officials and Qatari mediators were narrowing gaps on the MOU in Tehran. The same day Trump posted his Truth Social cancellation of strikes at 9:28 PM ET. The same day the narrative pause architecture came together.
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
A small but important sourcing caveat. Presidential determinations are sometimes drafted days before signature. The June 11 date is the signature date, not necessarily the drafting date. But the choice to release the document on June 16, exactly inside the Vance media tour window and exactly two days after the MOU signing, is the deliberate decision. Release timing is choreography. The administration chose to publicize the reload instrument inside the peace narrative cycle.
The signaling is structural. My framework includes a specific indicator I have referenced in prior pieces as “the loud peace, the quiet reload.” When a government simultaneously broadcasts diplomatic deliverables and quietly formalizes the industrial base for continued kinetic exchange, the operational interpretation is that the diplomatic deliverable is the narrative layer and the industrial base preparation is the structural layer. The structural layer is the one to believe.
The MOU text. Israel is not in it.
The Al Arabiya leak of the 14-point MOU text on Tuesday confirmed what the Jerusalem Post and Iran International had been reporting since the weekend. Israel is not mentioned in the document. Israel is not party to the agreement. Itamar Ben-Gvir confirmed Tuesday that the deal “does not bind us” and that Israel was “not party to this agreement.” Netanyahu reiterated Israel will “preserve its freedom of action” against Hezbollah in Lebanon.
The first point of the MOU calls for “an immediate and permanent end to the war on all fronts.” But Israel is not bound. Israeli forces struck south of Beirut on June 14 (the day the MOU was signed). Israeli forces remain in southern Lebanon. Israeli defense minister Israel Katz explicitly said Israeli forces will remain in the territory seized since the start of the war.
Refer a friend
This is the structural contradiction inside the MOU itself. The document calls for an end to fighting on ALL fronts. The party most likely to restart the fighting on the Lebanon front is NOT a signatory.

> This is the indicator I have referenced in escalation ladder assessments as “the missing signatory.”
When a peace document binds the negotiating parties but not the party most capable of rupturing the peace, the peace is structurally fragile by design. The fragility is the feature, not the bug. It preserves the option for renewed kinetic exchange through Israeli action that the US is not formally constrained to prevent.
The $300 billion fund and the protectionism counterweight
The MOU’s first point also references the $300 billion private investment vehicle for Iranian reconstruction. Per Reuters, this fund is not government money. It is private capital from the US, Gulf, Asia, South America, and Africa. It is separate from the $24 billion in frozen Iranian assets discussed in a separate point.

reads.title: Donald Trump turns on Israel
reads.subtitle: Not for the right reasons - but this is an opportunity
reads.body:
- Donald Trump has turned on Israel.
Not because he has a conscience or undergone a Damascene conversion. Let’s get that out of the way immediately: do not give this man any credit. Along with Joe Biden, Trump has armed and facilitated Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its other war crimes across the region, including in Lebanon. Mouthing off about Israel is one thing. Doing anything practical to stop its crimes is another.
But what Trump said at the G7 should still be understood for what it is: a confession. Before the cameras, he complained that Israel’s war in Lebanon has dragged on too long, and that “too many people are being killed.”
Then he said something striking:

> You don’t have to knock down an apartment house every time you’re looking for somebody. There are a lot of people in those apartment houses and they’re not all Hezbollah.
BattleLines with Owen Jones is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Trump here admitted that Israel - thanks to the weapons and support provided by the US - is destroying apartment blocks full of civilians.
Of course, the evidence for this is overwhelming.
That includes in Lebanon itself.
Take the Israeli attack on an apartment block in Ain El Delb in September 2024. The justification was that Israel was targeting a Hezbollah commander. The Israeli air raid hit the six-storey building, tipping it over down a hillside, killing 73 people and injuring 60 others. Of those killed, 23 were children.
AP carried the testimony of one survivor, who said it was worse than being trapped in a coffin.
The BBC also carried the story of Julia Ramadan, a young woman who was terrified about Israeli strikes in Lebanon and so went to stay at their family home in Ain El Delb, hoping for safety. She was killed.
In Gaza, this crime has been particularly widespread.
Share
The Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 magazine has extensively covered Israel’s destruction of entire residential blocks in Gaza in order to kill a purported Hamas military target - including Hamas targets of no military value, or people with no military connection branded as legitimate Hamas targets, or indeed people who have no connection to Hamas at all.
They covered one example in which the Israeli army authorised the killing of around 300 civilians to target a Hamas commander, involving the destruction of several large multi-story apartment buildings. “Entire families with children were killed,” as one paramedic they quoted tells them.
In another example, the Israeli army destroyed a high-rise building to try to kill Mohammed Shabaneh, a Hamas commander. They didn’t kill him, but they killed dozens of civilians.
So when Trump suggests Israel is destroying apartment blocks full of civilians, he is not revealing something new. He is saying aloud what the US administration knows to be true - as it delivers weapons and support.
Trump further said:

> I’m not happy with the way Israel has handled themselves with Lebanon and with Hezbollah. They should have been able to do the job faster. It just goes on forever. And when that happens, it throws a negative light on the big deal, and that’s the deal with Iran.
That’s not all. Following an Israeli attack on Beirut, Axios report that Trump told its reporter:

> Why did Bibi have to do a fucking attack? I was so pissed off. I let him know. He has no fucking judgement. I let him know that.
Subscribe now
At the G7 summit, Trump also said:

> Without the United States, there would be no Israel. Without me, there would be no Israel, because no other president was willing to do what I did.
It’s certainly true that Israel is dependent on US weapons, aid and support - whether that be subjugating the Palestinians, including occupation, apartheid and genocide, as well as invading and attacking Arab states.
Israel has received about a quarter of a trillion dollars in inflation-adjusted terms in US aid over the decades.
Trump also dismissed Israel as “the very small partner”.
What the hell is going on?
Trump has not suddenly been awakened to the horrors perpetrated by Israel. There’s a more straightforward explanation. He feels hoodwinked by Israel into launching a war he believed would be a devastating success, which has instead plunged his presidency into crisis, imposed mounting economic costs, and completely humiliated US power.
Trump further feels that Israel is now trying to sabotage attempts to end the war it promoted and which ended in humiliation for an already flailing superpower.
Indeed, the official agreement between Iran and the US represents a surrender by the aggressors .
It means the US signing up to such proposals as permanently ending the war, ending the naval blockade, a $300bn reconstruction plan for Iran, ending sanctions, and allowing the free export of Iranian oil.
As an article in Foreign Policy magazine puts it, it’s “a strategic calamity far greater than the U.S. defeat in the Vietnam War.”
Subscribe now
Obviously, Trump cannot admit to feeling tricked by Israel, because that would make him look extremely gullible and weak. After all, Israel did not force him to launch the war with him.
But this catastrophe offers an opportunity. In the US, public opinion has dramatically shifted against Israel. Among Democrats, that’s overwhelming - but it includes a majority of younger Republicans, too.
The US patronage of Israel could come to an end, and those who perpetrated terrible crimes could, in time, face justice.
That may once have seemed utopian. It no longer is.

reads.title: Palestine Action judge's insane suffragette claim
reads.subtitle: Her claim about the suffragettes insults our history
reads.body:
- Earlier this year, the high court ruled that the government’s banning of anti-genocide direct action group Palestine Action using anti-terror legislation was unlawful.
That has now been overturned by the Court of Appeal, who have ruled that the government’s ban is lawful. That means expressing support for Palestine Action can lead to a prison sentence of up to 14 years.
Palestine Action focused its actions against Israeli weapons firm Elbit, in the context of the British government facilitating Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people. Their proscription puts them on the same legal footing as ISIS and al-Qaeda.
Subscribe now
Thousands have been arrested for holding placards. As a result, as the i paper’s security correspondent Lizzie Dearden notes: “The average terror suspect arrested in England and Wales is now a white woman in her 50s as a result of the Palestine Action ban.”
But I want to focus on comments made by the lady chief justice, Sue Carr, as she read the judgment. She said:

> It is not, as it claims, a direct action civil disobedience protest group like the suffragettes operating transparently in the open. It is a covert organisation that operates using secret cells to avoid the detection and prosecution of those using violence to destroy the property of third parties. Palestine Action’s activities have caused injury as well as property damage.
What the hell is this judge talking about?
For a start, the suffragettes engaged in far more extreme acts than Palestine Action. The anti-genocide activists have smashed up the equipment of an Israeli weapons’ factory and thrown red paint at two RAF planes. One person has been convicted of GBH without intent after an altercation with a police officer.
The suffragettes planted bombs, burned down residential homes, attacked churches and schools and smashed up art galleries. Between 1913 and 1914, they were responsible for more than 300 incidents of arson and bombing.
They killed at least four people!
By any sane measure the suffragettes engaged in far more extreme acts than Palestine Action. Indeed their actions would unequivocally be criminalised as terrorism today.
Share
If the distinction is based on being covert or transparent, then it is as pedantic as it is ludicrous. Yes, the Women’s Social and Political Union ran a public-facing campaign, employed staff, organised huge demonstrations, and printed a weekly newspaper.
But when they were carrying out acts of sabotage or indeed violence, they were clearly not “operating transparently in the open”. They did so in secrecy, and many of the perpetrators were not caught.
The WPSU even had a secret group called the Young Hot Bloods which organised arson attacks, acid bombs, and attacks on homes.
Academic researchers who studied the suffragettes concluded that they became more covert in their final phase, meeting “the definitional criteria of what we call a ‘covert social movement network’ (CSMN).”
Palestine Action was a public-facing campaign with a website, social media accounts, press releases and a membership. It had two identifiable co-founders, Huda Amoori and Richard Barnard, who did public media interventions.
The lady chief justice has desecrated our history - and erased the truth about activists who fought for the rights of women like herself.
The proscription of Palestine Action is a sordid episode in our history, and marks our continued march towards authoritarianism. It is obvious what a Reform government would do with the repressive legal precedents and infrastructure it would inherit.
But we should note that proscribing dissident groups as terrorists is one hallmark of authoritarianism. Another feature is rewriting our past.
